subtopic: CANADA-U.S.-MEETING OF MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE ON JOINT DEFENCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CANADA-U.S.-MEETING OF MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE ON JOINT DEFENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to announce that there will be a meeting of the standing Canada-United States ministerial committee on joint defence on July 12 and 13 at Montebello, Quebec. This committee was formed some two years ago. As constituted, the Canadian members will be the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of Defence Production. The representatives from the United States will be the secretary of state, Mr. Herter; the secretary of the treasury, Mr. Anderson; and the secretary of defence, Mr. Gates.
The discussions will cover a broad range of questions affecting the joint defence of both countries. This will be the third occasion on which the committee has met.
As the house knows, it was established following discussions which I had with President Eisenhower in July, 1958. It was set up as a forum for periodic consultations on all matters affecting the joint defence of Canada and the United States. It reviews not only military questions but also political and economic aspects of joint defence problems. In the short period of its existence it has proven itself to be a valuable instrument for discussion of these problems at the ministerial level. It provides for that personal contact and better understanding which as a result have characterized meetings between representatives of our two countries.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CANADA-U.S.-MEETING OF MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE ON JOINT DEFENCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think all members of the house will welcome the announcement by the Prime Minister that this intergovernmental committee is to meet next week on mutual defence problems. There is no doubt that there are such problems, especially, if I may mention it, the problem of the use of nuclear weapons for defence and many others. If some of these problems can be cleared up at this meeting I think everybody will appreciate it very much.

subtopic: CANADA-U.S.-MEETING OF MINISTERIAL COMMITTEE ON JOINT DEFENCE
speechtext:

I can only express the hope that at this conference the government will take a position in the interests of Canada and will show a measure of independence that I think is very greatly required.

Mr. Chairman, in honestly discharging my duties as a member, it gives me pleasure to bring to the attention of the C.B.C. management a resolution sent to me by the Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste of the diocese of Joliette. It reads as follows:
Whereas, this year for the first time, the C.B.C. is promoting a country-wide contest for choral groups, a contest that will draw participation from hundreds of choral societies, involving thousands of Canadian residents,
Whereas the winners will be receiving only a small amount of award money,
Whereas such choral societies will include thousands of Canadian citizens who will have to put in several days work rehearsing the prescribed pieces,
Whereas although such choral societies will be amateur groups, we think the amount of the awards is ridiculous in view of the exorbitant fees being paid to performers who are not even Canadian residents and are in Canada just temporarily,
Therefore be it resolved that we, the directors of the Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste de Joliette Inc., on behalf of our thousands of members, urge the Canadian government to insist that the C.B.C. remedy the situation and that every member of those choral societies receive an amount comparable to the fee paid to foreign performers filling engagements in C.B.C. studios.
Mr. Chairman, I strongly urge the C.B.C. management to take note of that resolution and act accordingly.
We all know that today, radio and television broadcasts reach into every Canadian home, and that the programs have a strong impact on the minds of the Canadian people.
I wish to refer now to a seminar held last year at the social centre of the University of Montreal, under the auspices of the Holy Name societies.

Supply-C.B.C.
Following this seminar, a few resolutions were carried:
X. That a member of the clergy act as adviser to radio and T.V. producers when religious subjects are being presented.
2.	That an ethical code be drafted for the guidance of radio and T.V. producers.
3.	That no programs for adults be shown at hours when children may be listening to radio or watching T.V.
4.	That newspapers publish moral ratings of programs.
5.	That Catholic universities give courses to acquaint producers and actors with Catholic teaching.
Those resolutions were carried for a well known reason.
Nevertheless, I am convinced that the C.B.C. has helped foster national unity in Canada and I strongly urge the corporation to keep extending its French network in all areas where there are French-speaking minorities, and to extend its English network in the province of Quebec where there are English speaking minorities.
Ever since I have been a member of this house, I have found, to my surprise and puzzlement, that whenever members want information about C.B.C. administration or expenditures, they just cannot obtain details as to salaries or anything else.
As representatives of the people, we have a responsibility. Mr. Chairman, how can we adequately discharge that responsibility unless we get information in answer to our questions?
Mr. Chairman, I believe that this policy of silence is basically counter to our democratic system.
As I said earlier, the C.B.C., as such, has been of great service to Canadians, but I am not prepared to say that the organization is faultless. It is a human institution, and has shown serious deficiencies in the past. I am sure there still are deficiencies in the C.B.C. now. Besides, everybody is aware of the corporation's large deficits.
For those reasons, I would be very glad if the corporation were allowed to answer the questions on the order paper, or verbally asked by hon. members.
In view of those C.B.C. deficits, and of the attitude of the management who often refuse to answer our questions, I wonder if there might not be some way to drum a little sense into the bureaucrats, so that they might be fair to the representatives of the people.
Because of its deficits and of the inadequate supervision at times in certain fields,

by those responsible for the corporation, the C.B.C. has some similarity with the tower of Babel. That is why members of parliament have good reasons for asking questions, and have a right to do so. They should enjoy more power than the bureaucrats. They should be able to get answers to their questions, and the corporation should be able to supply details with regard either to salaries, remuneration or fees that are being paid.
It seems to me that we are responsible to the people, and if we really want to make some constructive criticism, we should have that information.
Mr. Chairman, I made those remarks without any bad intent, merely out of a desire to honestly discharge my duty as a representative of the people.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm allow me a question?
Certainly.

The point raised by the hon. member is of great interest to all of us. I wonder therefore if, at this stage of the proceedings in committee, the hon. member could not appropriately ask all questions he wants answered, since he has just indicated that he has been unable to obtain any answer from the present administration to the questions he had asked.
I therefore suggest to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montealm that he ask all his questions right now.
The hon. member should be addressing the chairman of this committee.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised to hear the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) ask me that question. As a member of the opposition he is certainly not in a position to answer on behalf of the corporation. I in turn suggest that he direct his comments to C.B.C. authorities.
Mr. Chairman, every hon. member knows that, last year, at the committee meetings, we were unable to get answers to the questions we asked with regard to certain commentators. When we asked what salaries or fees were being paid to some C.B.C. commentators, we were quite unable to extract that information, and the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont is perfectly aware of this fact. That was precisely the reason for the remarks I have just made.

Mr. Chairman, I was not here the other evening when the estimates of the C.B.C. were first discussed, and in a few minutes this morning I have been trying very hastily to find out what has already been said so I will not waste the time of the committee by repetition. The minister knows how much I hate repetition, but I think there are a few things that are going to need repetition before these estimates are completed.
It will not surprise the minister if I do not embark upon any general statement at all, because I want to deal with something which I regard in the first place as a shocking affront to parliament and, in the second place, as a clear breach of the law made by parliament. I intend at this stage of my intervention to deal exclusively with that subject. Since I have found that the most succinct account of what I have to say is contained in an editorial in the Toronto Star of September 12, 1959, it might avoid a certain amount of repetition if I simply read the editorial. I would point out, Mr. Chairman, that the editorial is not written about any debate that is going on in parliament. It is entitled, "Government Flimflam with C.B.C.", and reads as follows:
The Star understated the truth in writing last June 24 and subsequently that the threat of government domination of the C.B.C. endangered free speech on that network. There was then no longer a mere threat. The domination was a fact.
This was concealed by an elaborate government flimflam, disclosed only yesterday by a dispatch from Bruce Macdonald of the Star's Ottawa bureau. On June 24, Alphonse Ouimet was squeezed out as chairman of the C.B.C. board of directors and Ernest Bushnell as vice chairman; Robert L. Dunsmore was made chairman, and Charles Leeson vice chairman. Parliament was grossly misinformed about the switch, for as late as July 10 revenue minister Nowlan told the house that Mr. Dunsmore was acting chairman while Mr. Ouimet and Mr. Bushnell were on sick leave; and in its July 16 report, the commons broadcasting committee's report still took for granted that Mr. Ouimet and Mr. Bushnell were chairman and vice chairman respectively.
Supply-C.B.C.
When Mr. Nowlan did finally announce August 17 that Mr. Dunsmore had become chairman, he omitted the date of the appointment. To do otherwise would have revealed how he had misled parliament.
On June 24 mass resignations of the C.B.C. talks department were in full swing, protesting the cancellation of Preview Commentary's reports of parliament. Testifying to the broadcasting committee, the C.B.C. rebels said the threat "heads will roll" from high government quarters had brought on the censorship of that program.
Now we find that even while Mr. Bushnell was denying to the committee July 1 that he had ever been threatened that "heads will roll", his own head was off. Everything indicates that the dismissals of Mr. Ouimet and Mr. Bushnell from the board were a government power play, designed to bring the C.B.C. under its thumb. And the appointment of Mr. Dunsmore, with no visible qualifications, indicates the same.
Mr. Nowlan evidently has pummelled the C.B.C. into submission. For the fact is, Mr. Nowlan was not appointed as minister of the C.B.C.; he was appointed to report for the C.B.C. to parliament. It is parliament itself, and not the cabinet or any of its ministers, to which the C.B.C. is responsible.
Or should we say, was responsible? For Mr. Nowlan appears to be running the C.B.C. as if it were a department of government and under his direct orders. When a system of public communications such as television and radio is under domination of a government, then Canadians had better be on guard that it is not transformed into an instrument of official propaganda.
Now, sir, I want to review-
More Liberal propaganda.

The hon. member who is licking his wounds over there can get up and speak in his own time. I would recall to the minds of members of the committee, and especially the minister, that prior to July 10 of last year I had asked a question of the acting minister, the hon. member for Greenwood, because the minister was not in the house. The hon. member for Greenwood took the question as notice, and I want to emphasize the fact that the minister had notice of my question. He was not or ought not to have been taken by surprise. On July 10 of last year, as will be found on page 5777 of Hansard, I asked the minister this question on the orders of the day:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder If I could put a question to the Minister of National Revenue. Could the minister tell us who at the present time is performing the statutory functions of the president of the C.B.C. as chairman of the board of directors?
The minister replied:
Colonel Landry is, as I said, chairman of the management committee, and Mr. Dunsmore is chairman of the executive committee of the board of directors and in the absence of the vice president is acting as chairman of the board.
That is the information that was given to the house in response to a question of which

Supply-C.B.C.
due notice had been given to the minister. Then on August 17 there was an announcement that Mr. Dunsmore and Mr. Leeson had respectively been chosen as chairman and vice chairman of the board of directors of the C.B.C., but the date on which that had been accomplished was not given. I must say that until Mr. Macdonald published his story in the Toronto Star, or until he was preparing that story, it had never occurred to me that this act was other than something that had taken place in August or very shortly before. But it was drawn to my attention that in fact this election of Mr. Dunsmore and Mr. Leeson had taken place on the 24th of June, at the very height of the crisis in the C.B.C., when the committee was sitting and when surely the committee, in its investigation of this corporation, was entitled to be told what was happening at the very top, to be told that heads had already rolled at the very top.
Yet the whole of this information was kept completely secret from parliament; indeed, so secret that when the committee made its report to parliament it recommended as a change which it would be desirable to make in the future that the president should be relieved of his duties as chairman of the board and a separate chairman appointed. That was a recommendation the committee made which shows that, unless there was even more flimflam than we yet know, the members of the committee did not know anything about what had happened on June 24.
When I learned what had happened I was really very angry, as I think any member of parliament had a right to be, and as I think I had a special right to be because I was the person who had posed the question. I issued a statement to the press, and in order to be completely fair to the committee and the minister I intend to put it on the record now. I gave this statement on September 11 to the Toronto Star, which asked for it:
I do not object in principle to having a chairman of the C.B.C. board who is not the executive head of the corporation; in fact, 1 indicated on the last day of the session that might be some slight improvement. But I do object, anyone having any regard for the rights of parliament will object, to the C.B.C. board of directors making bylaws which change a law made by parliament, I object even more strongly to the fact that the Minister of National Revenue not only failed to disclose the truth to parliament in response to a direct question but gave an answer which was not true.
This is just the latest example of the contempt of the Diefenbaker government for parliament, about whose rights they were so insistent when in opposition. Obviously, they did not dare to tell parliament that heads had already rolled in the C.B.C. Nobody will believe that the CJB.C. board acted on its own in setting aside the law made by parliament and substituting its own bylaw.
[Mr. Pickersgill.j
Now, sir, we have had some very strange developments indeed. We had the minister saying that he was never told about this. I have a press clipping to this effect. It is from the Ottawa Journal of September 12, and the heading reads, "Didn't tell Nowlan of Top Level C.B.C. Changes".
Revenue minister Nowlan said Friday he was not advised by the C.B.C. board of directors at the time the directors changed their chairman.
This is in quotation marks, and my statement was issued on the 11th. I had not seen the minister's statement when I made my statement or I do not believe I would have put the last sentence in the categorical language which I did. I would have put in everything else, but not the last sentence. The minister said:
I don't know why they should have.
Well, I think I will tell the minister before I am finished why I believe they should have. He described it as a matter of the internal management of the board. Here we were with a committee which was going into the internal management of the C.B.C. and the minister felt the C.B.C. should not tell him of a fundamental change that was being made, indeed, a breach of the law.
Mr. Nowlan, who reports to parliament for the C.B.C., was commenting on a story in the Toronto Star that the public was denied information for eight weeks when C.B.C. president Alphonse Ouimet and vice president Ernest Bushnell were replaced as chairman and vice chairman respectively of the C.B.C. board.
The newspaper said that at a C.B.C. board meeting June 24 two C.B.C. directors, Robert L. Dunsmore of Montreal and Charles Leeson of Stratford, were named chairman and vice chairman. The appointments were not announced until August 17 when Mr. Nowlan issued a statement on the change.
Mr. Nowlan said Friday he did not learn about the change until he was asked.
Well, if the minister quarrels with that statement I would be happy to have him quarrel with it at once. If he does not, I assume that is the statement he wishes us to accept.
What did spokesmen for the C.B.C. have to say about this? Their public relations man made a statement in Halifax, and this appeared in the Ottawa Journal of September 12 also, the same day as the minister's statement. It reads: "C.B.C. Denies Board Hid Appointments". Well, I had better read the item, because we know that sometimes headlines are not entirely an accurate reflection of what appears under them.
Halifax, (CP):-Public relations director R. C. Fraser said Friday night the C.B.C. "emphatically denied" any implication that "something nefarious" occurred at a board meeting in Toronto June 24. Mr. Fraser was commenting on a Toronto Star story which said news of removal of president

Alphonse Ouimet and vice president Ernest Bush-nell as chairman and vice chairman respectively for the C.B.C. board of directors was withheld from the public for eight weeks.
Mr. Fraser said on June 24 Mr. Ouimet was recovering from a heart ailment and an operation and Mr. Bushnell, who had been acting president, was "on the verge of exhaustion."
Because of the necessity to have a presiding officer, Mr. Fraser said, the bylaws were changed to provide for the election of a chairman and vice chairman from among nine of the eleven directors.
Robert L. Dunsmore and Charles Leeson were elected to one-year terms on June 24.
Note that, sir; one-year terms; yet we were told on July 10 that they were merely acting during the incapacity of the president and vice president, which the board had a perfect right to do; that I do not question. What I do question is the board's usurpation of powers which were not given by parliament and, as I will show in a few moments which parliament did not at the time intend them to have.
The Star also said the June meeting followed by one day the levelling of charges of "clandestine political interference" against the C.B.C. and added that the election of Mr. Dunsmore and Mr. Leeson was not made public until August 17 by revenue minister Nowlan.
"The charges of political interference had nothing to do with the meeting," said Mr. Fraser. "The date had been set months before".
Mr. Fraser said the June changes were not considered news "because they made no change in the operating policy."
"If the Star had called us the next day we would have told them the story," Mr. Fraser said.
"There certainly has been no suppression."
I am not saying at the moment that there is a direct contradiction between that statement and the statement made by the minister, but I must say that when one takes these two statements together they seem to leave an implication that ought to be removed. What is even more serious, if possible, than that is that this whole possibility was envisaged during the debate on the bill. I wish to put on the record now from Hansard of August 26, 1958, at page 4139, an exchange which took place between my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition and the Minister of National Revenue, which reads:

May I ask, Mr. Chairman, whether it is the intention-I have not been able to find it in the provisions of this bill although it may be there-to provide that the president of the corporation should be the chairman of the board and preside over the meetings of the board? The minister has referred to him merely as the executive officer. But is he not also the chairman of the board and the one who presides over the board of directors?

I do not think there is a section spelling that matter out in detail in the bill. But I think it was taken for granted that where someone was not named chairman or if there was not a definite designation, the chairman would be the president.

That is true with regard to the board of governors; he is designated.
Supply-C.B.C.
Yes.
There is nothing in this bill to designate any member of the board of the corporation as chairman of the board?

That is right.
I want to be utterly and completely fair about this matter. I know that language is ambiguous, but there is a very important and very compelling precedent in connection with this matter. It so happened that a few years ago one of the chartered banks wished to choose one of its officers other than its president to be chairman of its board. The government of the day felt it necessary to ask parliament to amend the Bank Act expressly to provide that a bank could have a chairman of the board who was not the president. When these circumstances are taken together, the clear inference from the words of the minister in reply to the Leader of the Opposition, the clear inference that the president of the corporation was to be the chairman of the board, and the fact that parliament and the government of the day felt it was necessary to amend the Bank Act to provide specifically for a chairman of the board who was someone other than the president, there does not seem to be any room for doubt that this was clearly an infringement of the law.
I do not know whether Mr. Dunsmore or Mr. Leeson have received any special emoluments as chairman and vice chairman, but I think we are entitled to be told whether they have or not. I think we are entitled to an opinion, if they have, from the law officers of the crown as to whether that was a proper payment to be made out of the treasury.
They have not.

The minister, I understand, says they have not. Well, if they have not, that point does not arise. I think we are also entitled to have from the minister before these estimates are concluded, an opinion from the deputy minister of justice on the point that has been raised. If this point had not been raised at all in debate, if the inference had not been made, if the committee last year had not found it necessary to recommend a change in the law, thus indicating clearly what the intentions of parliament were at the time, there might have been some slight room for argument, although I suggest that in the light of the precedent in the case of the Bank Act there is not any real room for argument. There is nothing of which over the years, parliament has been more jealous, and properly so, except the independence of the judiciary and the courts, than the independence of the C.B.C. In view of the minister's denial in the press I am not asserting that

Supply-C.B.C.
the minister did know at all about what went on at that time, because I have never asserted that the minister-
I just received a note from Mr. Dunsmore saying that he did not know for some time either, because he was not at the meeting.

I must say that the minister has certainly not increased my confidence in the competence or the sense of the responsibility of the present directors of the C.B.C. by the statement he has just made. If at a time when there was a crisis all over the country about this matter, the C.B.C. board had so little sense of responsibility that it regarded this as a routine matter that did not even need to be reported to the minister, at a time when a committee was sitting and parliament was sitting and if, as I assume, the C.B.C. like other state agencies has someone who does read Hansard-and if they have not, they ought to have-and who is aware of what goes on, surely if they had any sense of responsibility they would not have left the minister in the position in which he found himself after he gave that answer on July 10. I would almost go so far as to say that if I had been the minister I would have thought whatever head was responsible for that situation ought to have rolled.
There would have been another head roll, eh?

It is certainly a display of a shocking sense of irresponsibility if the facts are as the C.B.C. and the minister have said they were, namely that they regarded this matter as pure routine; that when a question was asked in parliament they allowed the minister to make a statement which was not true and did not inform him of the truth so that he could correct that statement. I say that it gives us very scant ground for confidence in the competence of this board. I say moreover that when the situation was as it appeared in September, my view is that the board of the C.B.C. should have repaired the error and should have repaired it promptly. They should have announced that fact publicly and said they had made a mistake, that they were sorry for that mistake, and should have reinstated the president, who according to the statute passed by this parliament was intended to be chairman of the board, in the position which was rightfully his. It seems to me that this is not a trivial matter particularly in relation to the C.B.C. and in relation to broadcasting. Neither broadcasting nor the C.B.C. is an agency of the government. It is an agency of the state responsible directly to parliament and having a spokesman here.

I must say that in this particular respect, if I accept the minister's word, as I do, there is no way in which we can really hold the minister accountable. But that is all the more reason why we should know just what other things the C.B.C. board is doing that it regards as matters of routine that do not need to be reported to the minister and about which parliament can be left in the dark, such as deposing the president of the corporation and putting somebody else in his place who was never intended by parliament to be there.
Here we have this government, the members of which when in opposition ranted and roared about the rights of parliament and ranted and roared about adherence to statutes. Yet this is the kind of record we have. It seems to me that in the face of this kind of record we should be told by the minister, and told now, just what was done about this matter after September 12, when it certainly came quite forcibly to the minister's attention; what the present situation is, and whether the minister has any view from the law officers of the crown that the board had the power to do this act which on the face of it, and on the face of the minister's statement and on the face of the precedent I have cited, there does not seem to be any ground for suggesting that they had.
It surely is for parliament and not for the board of the C.B.C. to determine what shall be the constitution and structure of that board. If we are establishing boards that have so little regard for parliament and such an exalted view of their own functions that they think they can set aside the statutes and make other arrangements that may seem to them more convenient as a mere matter of routine, what else is happening?
Having put the case as bluntly and as accurately as I can from a factual standpoint, and having stated my position on it, I think I should allow the minister to reply.

I should like to take this opportunity to once again bring to the attention of the minister the fact that there are a large number of people in northern Manitoba who do not yet have the services of television. I refer particularly to the people in the area of The Pas and Flin Flon. These people in both these areas are recognized as being in the higher wage bracket in relation to other wage earners in Canada and, as I have mentioned previously on other occasions, they are paying a higher income tax than most other wage earners in Canada. Of course this income tax is partially going to support the C.B.C.
1 doubt very much whether there is any other place in Canada with such a concentrated population as there is in the town of Flin Flon that is not served by television. In this locality there are approximately 15,000 people in one concentrated group. I do realize that many other areas in Canada have populations possibly as large or maybe even larger when you take into consideration outlying areas, farming communities adjacent to towns, and so on; but Flin Flon has its group of people, as I mentioned before, concentrated in one small area. At The Pas much the same situation arises, although there is a somewhat smaller population.
I also realize that some of the areas in Canada which are currently being serviced have smaller populations, but they are in closer proximity to present C.B.C. facilities and therefore can be serviced at a lower cost per household. However, I would like to emphasize the fact that people in northern Manitoba and the particular areas I am speaking of, Flin Flon and The Pas, have pioneered that area and made their homes there. They have brought up their families and are developing the north. I think all hon. members will agree that, taking into consideration those facts, they should be given every possible consideration that the government or the C B.C. can give them.
I might say there are one or two other areas in northern Manitoba which also suffer from lack of good radio reception. In particular I mention Lynn Lake and the new townsite
Supply-C.B.C.
of Thompson. I had the opportunity of going into Thompson the other day, and I found it to be a fast growing community. They expect to have 8,000 to 10,000 people there in the next year and a half to two years, and they tell me that radio reception in that area is very poor. I did hear some talk that the C.B.C. were planning to put some sort of satellite in there to improve radio reception, and I certainly hope this talk is not just idle rumour but that plans are under way to do this not only at Thompson but also at Lynn Lake. Possibly the minister could give me some information about that matter.
While in Flin Flon I found that more and more people are leaving the northern areas because television is not available to them. To the people in the larger centres who accept television as a natural thing this might seem a little out of place, that people should leave good jobs with good security to go to another place where television is available. But when you stop to consider the educational value of television for growing children, and one thing and another, it is not too difficult to realize that if we do not show a greater interest in these places we are going to find it very difficult to keep key men in them.
On other occasions in this house the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has made a few inquiries about television in northern Manitoba, and on occasion I have suggested to him that this matter is being kept constantly before the minister and the C.B.C. not only by myself but by other federal members from Manitoba. I would suggest to him again that it might be a good idea for him to look after his own constituency. Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is asking us today to vote a sum of $71,739,400, covering the operating costs of radio and television services, those of the international service, and capital expenditures. The corporation, in making this request, is being modest and discreet. It does not want to bother the representatives of the people with trifles. Therefore it does not supply any details. No explanations are given. Hon. members and the government are merely implored to approve the C.B.C. budget.
It no doubt considers this as some transitory ordeal, and that while it faces the obligation once a year, or having its moment of truth, it is only a fair price to pay for the tranquillity it subsequently enjoys when it no longer has to give an account of its management and is free to do what it bally well likes with taxpayers' money.
Today it is paying its tribute to that democratic institution, the government, knowing full well that tomorrow it can go on lambasting it, to reply insolently to questions asked by the representatives of the people, and to snap its fingers at taxpayers' representations.
Indeed, Mr. Chairman, why should it worry about those things, since our laws authorize it to ignore those representations, because the C.B.C. is sovereign, and seems to have the added assurance of impunity.

That Mr. Chairman, is precisely the anomaly I would like to denounce once again before approving, and not necessarily with a light heart, the C.B.C.'s budget. I bear no grudge against it; on the contrary, I have on many occasions praised its achievements, and I am happy to pay tribute at this time to the eminent services the C.B.C. is giving the citizens of Canada.
However, I do find it abnormal, and contrary to the principles of responsible government, that the C.B.C. should not be obliged to give the government a more detailed account of its administration.
Nor do I accept, by reason of the same principles, that the C.B.C. should be a private preserve where unfortunately too often, favouritism-and since the word is currently in vogue-political patronage, reign supreme. As I have stated in the past, the C.B.C. is not a crown corporation like the others, precisely because it operates in the field of minds and consciences. Each of the services it provides cannot be appraised solely by administrative and financial standards.
On the other hand, the responsibility with which the C.B.C., has mistakenly been invested in the field of education compels us to scrutinize its programs with the greatest care, so that we can determine whether it respects the patterns and objectives assigned to our society by the philosophical, theological and moral principles which constitute the structure of our social life and the traditional basis of our teaching.
The services rendered by the C.B.C. may be classified under two main headings: information and entertainment. A third function, and one which-in view of the specific provisions of Canada's constitution-I can unhesitatingly describe as an usurped function, is that of education.
I have always been of the opinion that to entrust public information to a state organization is a very risky thing. Indeed the objectivity of that information rests on the good faith of the individuals, on their training and on the principles from which they seek inspiration. For, as often happens, those who dispense information betray their convictions, their principles and, frequently too, their political allegiance. News reports are therefore inevitably coloured, and this is understandably objected to by people who do not share the views of commentators, journalists and reporters. Private information agencies are obviously not immune to this danger, but since they are not being financed by the taxpayers, any erring ways that they can be accused of cannot fairly be imputed to the government.

In the field of entertainment, the C.B.C. does not yet seem to be sufficiently aware of the fact that it is the taxpayers who must pay the bills piled up by artists, producers, and employees of all kinds. The C.B.C. spends handsomely.
Producers undoubtedly mean well. They are trying to improve the program quality, to introduce new angles, to achieve originality and constantly to extend the field of artistic experiments of all kinds. But there is extravagance. There seems to be a prevalent belief that, in this field, Canada can afford to spend as much as do much wealthier countries. There are an increasing number of programs requiring expensive travelling; costly productions are prepared regardless of expense. From past experience, the firm conviction is held that members of parliament and the government will approve the corporation's actions without a second look.
The intention of providing entertainment and opportunities for mental relaxation may be quite sincere.
However, it must always take into account the realistic fact that all this has to be paid for by the people of Canada, they are the ones who foot the bills for the expensive shows put on by the corporation. They have no choice. They have no say in the matter of programming, nor can they refuse to pay the bill. Programs are thrust upon them, which they have to pay for. Now, in show business, the patron generally has the privilege of choosing the shows he wants to see. Especially has he the great privilege of not having to pay for those he has not chosen to see.
It will of course be objected that the corporation is trying to multiply its offerings to present a greater variety of programs, so as to allow televiewers a greater choice, one more in keeping with the diversity of tastes. All that is true; but, nevertheless, there remains the obligation for the public to pay for the whole thing. That is why I am advocating a closer supervision of expenses in that field, a supervision which can only be adequately ensured in compliance with the demands of responsible government, by the appointment of an advisory committee of citizens representing various categories of society, that would examine the various projects for C.B.C. programs, and would assess the possible costs, for report to the government.
Supply-C.B.C.
This would have the advantage of enabling the representatives of the people to exercise a discreet control on the spending of public funds, and also on the preparation of programs. It would in no way hamper the freedom of those whose job it is to set up programs, to devise shows, and to put them on the air. It would perhaps sometimes remind creators and performers that the expression of their talents remains unfortunately and more particularly in the case of the C.B.C.-dependent of the financial means available to the taxpayer.
As to the so-called educational programs, I said before what I thought of them. I want to repeat that, to my mind the C.B.C. is usurping the responsibilities of the educator. I, for my part, maintain that if we have to tolerate, for the time being-and I do not know for how long yet-that the C.B.C., which is an organization of the central government, look after education, its programs should be entirely prepared in close co-operation with the council of public education and with the recognized institution of learning in our province. It is also to be hoped that the responsibility of those programs will be entrusted to people, who, besides being endowed with the necessary competence and experience in the fields of broadcasting and television, would moreover have the necessary qualifications on the academic level, which are required of those responsible for teaching in this country. Thus, what I have called before the perils of improvisation would be avoided and people who are not qualified for employment in the teaching institutions of our province and in our country would thus be eliminated.
I would like to come back to some suggestions I made on April 9 last in a speech in this house. I suggested at the time that a minister of this government be immediately responsible both for the C.B.C. and the national film board, as well as for all other cultural organizations of the government.
I insist on that point, and to reassure the timorous, let me add first that while I think the various government cultural agencies should be placed under a responsible minister, it does not mean that I recognize or approve in principle the jurisdiction of the central power in cultural matters. I am simply looking at the factual situation, which some day or other we shall have to improve or drastically change. That will not stop me, when the

Supply-C.B.C.
occasion arises, from urging the Ottawa government to hand over to the provinces whatever responsibilities they are entitled to under the constitution. Let me stress also, for the benefit of those who are always looking for a weak spot, that placing responsibility for the C.B.C. under a minister would not place the corporation in a strait-jacket and would not open it to political influence any more than the existence of a provincial secretary in Quebec places educational institutions in a strait-jacket or lays them open to the tyranny of politicians. Such a move would enable the government to examine the operations of the C.B.C. and, where necessary, to place financial limitations on its activity.
I have also suggested that the minister be assisted by a special deputy minister who would ensure liaison between the minister and the corporation. I think an English speaking deputy might be appointed for the English network, and a French speaking deputy for the French network. Incidentally, I think the practice of appointing two deputies, one for each language, should be applied to all departments. As to the French network, I consider it most important that a French speaking deputy minister be appointed. A man imbued with the French spirit, culture, outlook and with the basic principles of our French traditions, would be in a better position to understand the problems involved in the operation of the French network of the C.B.C. That would avoid the problems, misunderstandings and difficulties of all kinds arising from the impossibility for someone foreign to our language, culture and ideas to understand the particular conflicts arising within the C.B.C. French network.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to renew the other suggestions I made in the speech I delivered in this house on April 8 last. I add this: I urge the government to set up a royal commission to investigate the administration of the C.B.C., for the following purposes:
First, to consider C.B.C. finances; second, to stop unwarranted expenses; third, to examine the problem of salaries, security and stability of employment, and to define the duties and functions of every class of C.B.C. employee; fourth, to ensure objectivity in news reporting; fifth, to review the principles which should underly C.B.C. programs, and to bring about policies more consistent with the task originally assigned to the C.B.C.; sixth, to do away with all patronage and political interference.

Mr. Chairman, the suggestions I had put forward have been favourably received in the province of Quebec. In my own constituency, I have received many testimonials in that regard. I renew my plea at this time, and further, I urge the government to set up a royal commission as soon as possible, because I feel that the citizens of this country, whom it is our responsibility to represent, have for years been demanding such an investigation into the administration of the corporation.
The purpose of such an investigation, as I see it, should not be to place anyone in hot water, to hunt up scandals or to put people on trial for their opinions, but it should involve a close examination of the C.B.C. administration, so that once and for all, the people may find out in detail how the C.B.C. spends public funds.
Mr. Chairman, I would have hoped in this speech to examine certain other problems which I feel the government should look into. However, I shall let the matter rest.
In closing, I again urge the government, my government, to consider the possibility of allowing the taxpayers and their representatives to look into the administration of the C.B.C.
In this way, when the legitimate representatives of the people again go before the people, they will be in a position to answer all questions which the public is entitled to ask, and to give adequate answers, answers obviously more accurate and satisfactory than those given us so far.

Mr. Chairman, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its predecessor have long been of interest to members of this party, as to other Canadians, because we see in it an expression and development of Canadian nationalism. We are very concerned today over the position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am concerned not only with the general attitude of the people who are running it, but I am bothered by my own attitude. In the opinion of many people the corporation has deteriorated, and they have grave doubts about the service that the organization is performing and of its program standards. There are many doubts about its future and about its fundamental role of providing some kind of broadcasting service to the people right across the nation not only in metropolitan centres.

I hope the hon. member for Churchill and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate do not mind these remarks. I am not sticking my nose into Churchill but I know that if as the result of a policy decision, the constituency of Churchill receives what the hon. member is searching for, it will also bring services such as he wants to the part of the country that I represent. I think he should look at it not so much from the point of view of keeping our noses in our own constituency's business as asking for and expecting from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation a policy that will move it toward the attainment of a genuine national service to all the people.
Not very long ago in the house I made some criticisms of the C.B.C., especially in relation to the decision of the board of broadcast governors to allow the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to establish a television station in Edmonton. My argument was similar to that of other members, that before this rather large capital expenditure should be contemplated the C.B.C. should have gone farther in giving service to those areas that do not now have any television service at all and in many cases very bad or poor radio service. Since my remarks on that occasion I have been rebuked not only by some people in general but also by some of the C.C.F. party supporters in the west, who feel it is almost a question of desperation that those areas not only have private outlets but that they should have the opportunity to look at the kind of programs the C.B.C. produces.
In replying to these people I can only say that in my judgment, and I think in the judgment of the party, it is a difficult problem deciding which comes first, which is of primary importance. Perhaps because of the problems and needs of my own area I tend to feel that what should come first is the extension of some kind of service, even a minimal service, to everyone in the country. The argument that is always put forward by the broadcasting corporation officials to whom I talk is that there is the matter of cost, that you get into inordinate costs when you serve sparsely settled areas.
The corporation responds to this problem by establishing a formula of so much per capita or so much per household, and when an area reaches the population concentration that brings it under this formula the corporation then decides to go ahead. I know the corporation has shifted its formula to a certain extent in the last few years, but I should like to suggest it needs to shift it even more and look at the question of whether it should expand its facilities any further in metropolitan areas. There is nothing we can do now with respect to Edmonton, because
Supply-C.B .C.
they are going to go in there. I am talking even about the programming facilities, such as the provision of new studios in metropolitan areas, when there is still an important segment of the Canadian people who do not have any television service. As I look at the national needs this is most important.
The hon. member for Churchill mentioned people moving out of a region. In a country like ours where we do have mobility it may seem sad, but an amenity or a luxury or even a necessity from any point of view such as television does determine the attitude of people. I know that one of the difficulties many men have in the hinterland region is to keep their wives and children happy in a remote area where this kind of service is not available. It may be a commentary upon our civilization and the sad state it has reached, but this is so. I agree with the hon. member for Churchill that it is a very real problem.
I have pointed out to the house before that there is an inordinate requirement in the hinterland region for this sort of thing. People living in small bush communities who are keeping our basic and primary industries going, such as pulp and paper and mining, do not have the advantages of people in metropolitan areas such as Toronto, Ottawa or Montreal. There are not the leisure-time facilities. There is a remarkable lack of recreational facilities, especially for children and women. The people of the frontier have always been good at devising their own entertainment and educational opportunities, but with the present sophistication of society and young people it is very hard to support a really going community that does not have modern services such as television.
I can see this very definitely in another way that is connected. I refer to those subjects of interest that make us Canadians, and by way of example I point to the sports field. I have known railroaders to come from away up and down the line years ago in order to cluster in a small town and listen to a hockey broadcast. I know that hockey, football and other Canadian sporting events that have been and are carried by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation mean a great deal in tying the country together, just as the national news telecast means a lot. If we are going to have a continuation of the very vague situation where these people cannot know when they are likely to get some kind of service. I can only say that we as their representatives have failed to put over the urgency and the real need of the situation.
This leads me into another aspect of criticism that we have of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, one that has to do with programming. Perhaps I have been guilty

Supply-C.B.C.
as other members of the house in sounding off about programs. However, I have tried not to sound off about programs in particular but programming in general. I suppose the problem can be put in its extreme case in relation to the trans-Canada radio network and the fact that there are a number of low power relay stations in my constituency that carry its programs. In communities such as Marathon and White River this tends to be about the best radio reception they can get, because of the great amount of interference in trying to pick up United States stations, largely caused, I understand, because of iron formations and other natural phenomena.
The trans-Canada network programming tends to be what one would call heavy. I do not think it is quite in the category of the C.B.C. third program, but it is still a remarkably heavy diet. While I or other people may enjoy parts of it, and I have said so again and again, in the main the programming is quite unsatisfactory to many of the people who are captive listeners. It is far too heavy a diet for the kind of person living in our frontier communities. In saying this I am not in any way slighting these people, but merely pointing out that their tastes are not the tastes of the educated elite that one may find in a metropolitan area.
I sometimes think that the programming of the C.B.C., particularly on radio and to a degree on television, is oriented to an audience that the producers of the corporation envisage as in a metropolitan area. I sometimes think the public affairs producers have in mind those people who are influenced by and are in touch with all the media that metropolitan areas offer, but the people in the hinterland across the nation who are far away from metropolitan centres do not have this point of view. I can never get excited about Bach or Beethoven or any of the other musical greats, but I know that in the larger cities especially there is a great and developing appreciation of these composers. I also know that there are those who, so far as public affairs are concerned, are interested in international matters, but continually the C.B.C. emphasizes this external material or material that is cultural in a very highbrow way.
As a consequence, the impression gained of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation across the line is not that Canadians are more of the folksy or homey kind you see on Don Messer's program, but rather that they may be more like Lister Sinclair or Nathan Cohen. With all due respect to these gentlemen, they are hardly typical of the kind of Canadians and the interests of Canadians in areas distant from these metropolitan sophisticates.

I should like to think that the C.B.C. could lighten the programming on its trans-Canada network radio service. In saying this I do not want to convey the idea that the programs are not worth while, but I would suggest that they go over the heads of many people. Certainly many them find not worth listening to. I suggested before that it would be to the advantage of many of these areas if the programs that go out on the dominion network were available as a matter of choice, ahead of the trans-Canada network programs.
In so far as the television aspect of programming is concerned, I should like to appeal to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to take a good look at what the United States networks do in the field of public affairs. We have a tendency to belittle the accomplishments of the United States and to think they are all for whoop-de-doo and razzle-dazzle. I find that whenever I am in areas in which United States television programs can be received I get much stimulation in the field of public affairs; there is more excitement and real interest, and actually more coverage of domestic points than we get from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I have already expressed the view that I certainly think this represents a lack of stomach on the part of the C.B.C. It may be caused by the fact that there is a lack of imagination toward domestic affairs and a feeling that what the United States does would be dangerous to the position of the C.B.C. Well, I should like to think that Canadians had not only more guts than that, but more interest in their own affairs than the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation programming would indicate.
The argument I have had from C.B.C. producers-I think I am being fair to them- is, what is the point of concentrating on domestic public affairs, since most people in Canada are apathetic about them? You are never going to shake apathy unless you offer the people something, and the fact that the people to the south of us are not apathetic in the development of public affairs programming should be some encouragement to the C.B.C. I would hate to think that these private networks which are in the future, and for which the board of broadcast governors is projecting some ground rules, would become, as is entirely possible, the best medium we have for finding out about ourselves as citizens. I think that could very well come about unless the C.B.C. shows some imagination and leadership in that field.
One of the things I have noted is that in certain areas where you have private television stations with a responsible attitude toward their duties-I am not going to single

out any because I could also think of some examples of stations which have not responsible attitudes-you have a livelier sense of the community and what is going on, and the reaction of the community to the medium is better than we get from the C.B.C. I can give one example in my own area. The programming that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation puts into Port Arthur appears to come from some distant organization. This is a lack in the C.B.C. If the only time our particular region is ever noticed by the C.B.C. is when an elevator falls into the lake, then the C.B.C. is doing nothing to bring ours and other areas together nationally. We should discontinue the orientation toward large centres, such as Toronto, and the feeling that really life in Canada is concentrated in such centres.
The exhortation I would give to the C.B.C., and exhortations are popular these days, would be to get out in a programming sense and do a job for this Canadian nationalism that exists. Do not be frightened by controversial topics. However, they do not have to be in areas such as divorce to get the kind of controversy that Canadians really want to hear about. I can think of many Canadian problems about which the people would like to hear, especially what comes up in relation to the United States and the rather latent United States pressures that are bubbling to the surface. We never get much treatment of subjects of that kind.
It seems to me that last year the minister hinted that there would be a new look at the position of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation after the nine private television stations were set up. I have here his speech from last year. I would not like to read too much into it in this regard, but I certainly feel that he indicated that once this trend had solidified the government might consider, or there might be a reconsideration, of the kind of service the C.B.C. should give. Now, the Globe and Mail of Toronto has been arguing one aspect of this matter, and that is that perhaps the C.B.C. should be divorced from control or ownership of any facilities at all, and that it should be put in the position of a program agency in the public affairs field, not in the entertainment field; that as such it would carry out the old role of the cultural dike against the United States tide.
One of the other possibilities-I have heard this put forward by both Conservative and Liberal members in private-is that perhaps we should consider completely disposing of the C.B.C. when the set-up is complete. These are the two alternatives. I think I would have liked to see the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation left intact and engaged to do a much bigger chore. However, the policy has
Supply-C.B.C.
been set and we are following a trend. I would think that the experience in Britain has indicated that a vigorous public agency and vigorous private agencies can co-exist and offer a great deal of variety and a wealth of information in so far as the radiotelevision media go.
The party which I represent feels very strongly that the C.B.C. is in some danger from these alternatives. We do not think they are the right ones. I feel personally-I do not know how many members of my party feel this way-that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation by sheer lack of initiative, by failure to move, by lack of imagination, by always muffing its chances and looking like a fool in so many instances, will create the very kind of condition which will lead either to its destruction or to a very great narrowing of the functions that it carries out. For these reasons we would appeal to the corporation officials to get on their horse and start riding in the direction I have indicated.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate went into a lot of detail about one rather narrow aspect of the board of directors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I agree with most of what he had to say. I am not going to cover the same field, but I am very much bothered about the legality of the Dunsmore appointment. I should like a full explanation from the minister about it. I may say in this regard that most of us in this house have a great deal of respect for the minister. I have noted his tactics not only on this occasion but at other times. He is very quick to get to his feet. He never gives a full statement to start with on anything. However, I should like to say to him that what he fails to do in so far as the C.B.C. and the board of broadcast governors are concerned is to give us a thorough review. It seems to me any minister is faced with two alternatives in this house. He can come in and give such a thorough review that the opposition tends to be overwhelmed by detail and at least to have very few points on which it can criticize; or he can do as the minister usually does, namely sit in the bush. I would suggest that I would greatly appreciate from him-and I am not saying this from the point of view of needling him-a thorough review of this changed program and where they are going.
I think it is regrettable that we do not have the annual report of the C.B.C. I should like to know from the minister whether he now

has it in his hands, and whether he has in his hands a report from the board of broadcast governors, In the case of the board of broadcast governors it is most regrettable, because they have had a most exciting year, a most controversial one. They have been issuing orders and ukases and regulations in great numbers. They have been hiring employees. There has been more controversy and discussion about it than about any other government agency. I think it would have been of great service to us if we could have had the report before us.
The broadcasting committee has been set up, and I am going to vote or try to vote or move, when the committee starts, that the committee end; because I feel, and I know some other members have the same feeling, that now at this particular stage of the session, when we are sitting these long hours and are sitting through the lunch period, is not the time for us to get involved with private broadcasters, with the C.B.C. or the
B.	B.G.
It is not because we do not want to take a took at them. I should very much like to have a chance to analyse what Mr. Brown of the
C.	A.B. is going to say, and what the independent private stations are wanting to say. I may say frankly to the minister that I am greatly bothered about the role of government and the role of parliament in relation to these two agencies. The phrases are tossed around that the C.B.C. does not report to the government; that the minister is only, one might say, an echo chamber through whom the C.B.C. speaks; that parliament is the body to which the C.B.C. goes, and that parliament has final control over the C.B.C. It is even arguable that since we have had a select committee on broadcasting, this committee as a microcosm of the house has a responsibility toward the C.B.C. and the B.B.G. that is greater than that of the government itself.
I think we are in great confusion about the relationship of these two agencies to parliament. I believe in going so far as to advocate that we never have a question raised in this house about the C.B.C. or the B.B.G., but

instead have some kind of regular meetings between officials of these agencies and the parliamentary committee. When I speak of regular meetings I mean possibly two or three times a year. I do not think it does much for either the B.B.G. or the C.B.C. to have members such as myself getting up and asking questions about details, about programming or any other inquiry we may want to make. But I certainly think we have to keep up that kind of practice unless we can get some clear indication of just how parliament controls the C.B.C. and the B.B.G.
This relationship of government corporations and parliament is one of the most ambiguous ones of which I know. We have had several examples this session, in connection with the national harbours board and the Canadian National Railways, which pinpoint the difficulty. I have not met many members of this house, except perhaps the hon. member who has just taken his seat, who really want to gouge their thumbs into the C.B.C. or any other government corporation. I should like to know how the report is working out, and I especially want to know from the minister how I got this answer in relation to my question when I had before me clippings from the Winnipeg Free Press and the Winnipeg Tribune indicating that Mrs. Aitken had given a full report to the press as to how her activities in this particular field were going.

It will be recalled that when public broadcasting was first decided upon in this country it was done by the government of Mr. R. B. Bennett in the 1930's as a result of the recommendations of the Aird commission, in order to preserve a separate Canadian nationality in this country. That is why it was done, as hon. gentlemen who may not know much about it can find out by reading some of the speeches at that time. When it was done it received the very strong support of Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. Ernest Lapointe. It was made very clear at that time and by every royal commission and every parliamentary committee from that time until very recent times that what we wanted to be sure of was that the broadcasting authority, whatever it was, would have financial independence from the government; that we had to have a public broadcasting body, not because we believed in public ownership rather than private ownership but because we believed that Canada should be and should remain a separate country, and this was the only way that it seemed practical to do it in this field.
That is why it was done. But if public broadcasting, which anybody who lived through the 1930's, anyone who was an adult in the 1930's, knows is one of the most potent

instruments of tyranny and enslavement that has ever been invented, was to exist it must be surrounded with every kind of safeguard to see that what the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere seems to want to have happen in this country never should happen; in other words, to see that it was kept completely independent of the government of the day.
That was why we had the licensing system originally, and it was a very awkward way of financing broadcasting. It was certainly not very popular, and that was why the Massey commission recommended other financing methods which were for a fixed period of time, longer than the life of a single parliament. That was a wise move, even in those days when governments did not change so frequently as they seem to be doing more recently.
As I say, the idea was that there should be a fixed income, an income not under the control of the government of the day though ultimately, of course, under the control of parliament by statute, to be settled here in the open by parliament and not behind the closed doors of treasury board; settled in the open in parliament so the corporation would know what its income was, that it would not get any more if it pleased the government and it would not get any less if it displeased the government. That is the only safe way to have public broadcasting, because this could be a very dangerous instrument of tyranny indeed in the hands of certain people.
Some of the friends of some of the hon. gentlemen sitting in some parts of this house, and not here, seem to want that kind of thing if one can judge from a recent provincial election. Mr. Chairman, if this situation exists, I must tell you that there is a French proverb that says: "The hen that cackles is the one that has laid an egg".
