Mr. Chairman, I shall be reasonably brief because in a few minutes time I have an appointment with the public body with whom we are now dealing so that I may express my views on one of the great issues of our time. As I listened to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate wax eloquent in his somewhat overzealous wrath against any suggestion that freedom of speech be curtailed on the C.B.C. it brought to my mind one of the problems with which the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is faced, not only in Quebec but in other parts of Canada as well. I refer to its choice of commentators. I would be the last person in the world to suggest there should be any curtailment of the right of a man or woman to express views on the radio or television.
I think the point that was made and was misunderstood perhaps by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-I refer to the point made by the Quebec members-was that they feared that a clique had set in in the province of Quebec and that much of the public opinion or most of it was coming from Liberal sources. I agree with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate that Liberals, Tories, C.C.F. or what have you should be allowed to express opinions. However, I also think the C.B.C. should be extremely careful to take care that both sides of the question are presented and not just one side.
I was also interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur and the suggestion that the C.B.C. had a certain lack of stomach in the matter of promoting Cana-dianism through its "Viewpoint" and other

programs. I must say that with the hon. member's views I fairly well agree. I think we can turn on the C.B.C. and see fine programs from that body on the latest development in Algeria, in other Mediterranian countries, in Europe or in the United States of America but that we do not get in this country enough commentary on things that count in our own Canada.
For example, I am sure there will be a lively election issue in British Columbia later this year. I should like to think that sitting in Nova Scotia at that time I would be able to turn to television or to radio and get some fairly good reports on the issues in that election, to see not just one commentator make a five minute appearance on it but rather three or four. If necessary, the commentators could be labelled in this way: this person will give the Liberal viewpoint, this one the Conservative viewpoint, this one the Social Credit viewpoint and this one the C.C.F. viewpoint. But let us get the word from British Columbia into other parts of Canada. I think that is a serious criticism, namely that we see many broadcasts on public issues but unfortunately they* are the public issues of what is real at the moment in the United States or real at the moment in France and not enough on what is real at the moment in Canada. I hope the C.B.C. will be able to come up with a more acceptable formula.
It rather gripes me-and this is only a personal complaint-to see "Viewpoint" transferred so often to New York for reports by professors from Columbia University. I am sure we have in this country a great pool of able commentators which has not even been tapped by the public broadcasting system.
I should not like to leave this particular portion of my remarks without complimenting the C.B.C. for what I regard as a very fine step in their Canadian coverage, namely the appointment of Mr. Norman DePoe to Ottawa and his frequent appearance on news broadcasts to say what is going on in this chamber, in the other place and in parliament as a whole. I think that was a first rate step forward. I think he is discharging what could have been an extremely difficult responsibility with remarkable ease and also with remarkable non-partisanship. This type of appointment not only deserves the thanks of all but it also proves that it can be done, and done well, when the C.B.C. turns its attention to building up things that are Canadian.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made a suggestion that the C.B.C. be placed on a fixed budget for say the next

lour or five years. While I think this suggestion has some merit in it, I would humbly submit that perhaps this may be a year too early to bring it in for the simple reason that there will be private television stations in operation in different parts of Canada in competition with C.B.C. outlets which up to now have enjoyed the market solely. I rather suspect that instead of the $71 million we are going to be asked to vote this year we may be asked to vote a considerable bit more money next year unless the C.B.C. is able to get out and scrap more vigorously for the advertising dollar. I hope they will forget all ideas about peaceful co-existence with the private camp when it comes to getting the advertising dollar and that they get all they possibly can for themselves.
In the broadcasting committee last year I raised the suggestion to the then manager of the C.B.C., namely Mr. Bushnell, that it might be a useful idea to appoint salesmen on commission to obtain this advertising revenue. He thought it was a good idea and said he would look into it. Perhaps when the minister rises to reply to the various suggestions that have been made by hon. members he might let us know whether this in fact is being done.
I am a little bit disappointed at what I think is perhaps a lack of an obvious source of revenue for the C.B.C. and that is their venture this year once a month, or perhaps more than once a month, into the Game of the Day baseball broadcasts on Saturday afternoon. I think most of us are very happy to have these games presented instead of the inevitable cowboy and Indian hassle that usually comes on at that time. But in the ordinary ball game of nine innings-and when I say "the ordinary ball game" I am not thinking of what took place on the lawns of parliament the other night because that was extraordinary-there are in effect 17 or 18 intermissions, each one capable of carrying a one-minute spot and therefore each one capable of bringing in a great deal of revenue. I have noticed in Halifax on the C.B.C. there when the game was carried and again in Ottawa when the game was carried that there are a number of public service announcements-and with those I do not quarrel-but not enough revenuebearing messages. I think there is a natural opportunity for the C.B.C. to turn some aggressive salesmen loose in this city and in other places and really bring in a "whack of dough" for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. May I say to you, Mr. Chairman and through you to the minister and through the minister to the C.B.C.-that is the chain we are working on at the moment-and through the C.B.C. down to the salesmen I
Supply-C.B.C.
have in mind, that I hope this will be done and that the C.B.C. will be more aggressive about getting that revenue.
Finally, if I may, I should like to turn to something at home. The eastern section of Halifax county is currently poorly served by television. That is a problem that may be straightened away by the second television station in Halifax or it may be straightened away by the erection of a television station in Antigonish. Of this I am not sure, and I suppose nobody can be sure until the other television stations start operating. I know that Mr. Briggs' successor in the maritimes, namely Mr. Kennedy, has put forward the case for a satellite in the eastern end of Halifax county for Musquodoboit valley down through Mushaboom, Sheet Harbour, Necum Teuch, West Newdy Quoddy and Ecum Secum. When he brings this request to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and through them to the minister and through him to the treasury board to take action I hope that this time the people of that section of Halifax will emerge with their satellite television station. I shall not keep Mr. DePoe waiting. I thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

I could well associate myself with some of the remarks that have been made by the hon. member for Halifax, Mr. Chairman. I also believe that one of the main tasks of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in Canada is to bring Canada to Canadians. We live in a country of large extent and it may be possible that only a very small percentage of Canadians who live in one area of Canada know all ten provinces of Canada or very much about them first hand. For example, we talk about the tourist industry and encourage our people to visit various parts of Canada so that they will come to know Canada. These things are certainly very fine, I am sure we will all agree, but on the other hand it may at the same time be possible to bring to many Canadians most interesting information concerning other parts of Canada by means of radio and particularly television.
What I want to say at this time does not deal with the type of program which is given over television in Canada; my problem concerns those areas for which no service is provided, and I should now like to bring to the attention of the minister three points which are of interest to the people of my own constituency.
I would refer first to the C.B.C. radio station CBY at Corner Brook, Newfoundland. I have mentioned this problem in the house on two previous occasions and have brought it to the attention of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, but no action has been

Supply-C.B.C.
taken. Before confederation the radio station which existed at Corner Brook was one which serviced the whole west coast of Newfoundland. The radio station serves an area of 100 miles south of the station and about 200 miles to the north of the station to northern Newfoundland. Before 1949 this area was completely served by the local station at Corner Brook. In 1949 the station was taken over by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which carried on its radio duties.
In an area where communications are not all that could be desired radio plays a very important part. It is able to give service to people which no other means of communication can provide. In many of the fishing communities along the coast the people are interested in the movement of boats, particularly those boats which deal directly with their means of livelihood. This information was broadcast to these people by sponsored programs that in the main undertook to provide for the people of that area the information in which they were interested.
Then a couple or three years ago, I am not sure of the exact date, radio station CKEC was set up at Newcastle, New Brunswick, and operated on the same frequency, 790 kilocycles, as CBY at Corner Brook. I hasten to point out that I am not complaining about the station at Newcastle, New Brunswick. I know too that any interference that the one station may have with the other is not in the protected area of station CKEC in Newcastle or within the protected area of CBY at Corner Brook; but it so happens that the further you get away from the city of Corner Brook the greater is the interference of CKEC with CBY, with the result that 50 miles north of Corner Brook and 50 miles south it is almost impossible to understand the reception received. This is entirely due to interference from CKEY.
What the remedy is I am not sure, whether it is a matter of changing the ground pattern, whether the frequency should be changed, whether the station at Corner Brook should be made more powerful. I do not know the answer to this question and I will leave it to the engineers of the C.B.C. who are competent to give an answer. But I contend that a station Which has served people for years before Newfoundland came into confederation should be able to continue serving these people and not be interfered with by another station on the mainland of Canada. I say again, that I do feel these people have been deprived of the service to which they have been used for many years by interference from this particular station.
Radio station CBY is the only station on the west coast of Newfoundland. It is true

that people within the area are able to listen to stations in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and most of the time I understand are able to get some of the radio stations at St. John's, Newfoundland, but they are unable to receive broadcasts from the radio station at Corner Brook. Everybody knows that there is a complexion about a local radio broadcast that is important to the people in the area and perhaps not at all important to people outside the area. One of the things for which I would commend the C.B.C., as they have operated in parts of Canada that I know, is that they have been able to adapt themselves to the needs of the people in the area. I think that is a commendable thing. It has certainly been done in Newfoundland, but it would be much more effective if the area which is covered by station CBY could receive reception from this station without interference from the station at Newcastle, New Brunswick.
As I have said before, I have brought this problem to the attention of the minister on two previous occasions and I would hope that some serious consideration will be given to it. I know that at the moment some inquiries are being made. Similar inquiries have been made before but have not resulted in any remedial action. Therefore I would suggest to the minister that some careful consideration be given this problem.
I was interested in the statement which the minister made, I think on Wednesday evening, when he said that 94 per cent of the people in Canada were receiving radio broadcasts.
Television.

Television. I think that is a tremendous achievement, but I feel that the people living in this particular area are not receiving the service to which they are entitled from a national system of radio broadcasting. So again for the third time I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and I hope it will be possible this time to find some remedy.
I would now like to make some reference to the television station at Harmon Field, Stephenville, Newfoundland. I am not going to go into the set-up of the station. This is well known to the minister and his officials and they are well aware of the agreement which exists between the Canadian government and the United States government for the operation of this television station at Harmon Field which also gives television coverage to the very important town of Stephenville and the nearby air field.
However, on the Port au Port Bay peninsula there is a large number of people, and toward the south in the district of St. George's and the Codroy valley there is another large

body of people who are unable to receive television broadcasts from the station at Harmon Field. Only a year or so ago I could not have brought this problem to the attention of the minister for the reason that that area was not serviced by electricity. Not all of the area is served now but the service to that area is gradually being increased. I believe that with the possibility of receiving electrical services the coverage offered by the station at Harmon Field should be increased. I have discussed this with the United States officials at Harmon Field and they have intimated to me that they would be very willing to enter into discussions with the C.B.C. in order to make it possible for an increased number of people to receive television programs from the station.
My third point is to make some reference to the coverage of the television station at Corner Brook. This station is only about two years old and is rapidly becoming an important part of communications in the area. I can tell the minister right now that it is doing an excellent job. It has taken time for the station to acquire all the necessary instruments and local information that is required for the operation of the station but the station is to be commended for its work and it is giving a very fine picture to the people who are able to receive the program.
Those of us who come from Newfoundland like, of course, to see the Canadian hockey games. We enjoy them very much. Others of us like to see the boxing bouts on Friday night. Being a politician I suppose that I, too, have a natural interest in seeing two fellows knock each other around. Many of the programs from the mainland that are received in Corner Brook are thoroughly enjoyed.
On the outskirts of Corner Brook there is a large area which is not now receiving a satisfactory picture. I refer particularly to three places. I wish to refer first to the organized community of Steady Brook and the larger organized town of Deer Lake. These two areas are not now receiving satisfactory programs from the station at Corner Brook. What the solution is so these people will be able to receive the programs is one for the engineers to determine. It may well be that at Steady Brook and at Deer Lake some instrument such as a reflector will be necessary but in any event I would bring to the minister's attention the need for television coverage in that area. I hope it will be possible to have the difficulties investigated and the remedy provided.
Slightly to the north and west of Deer Lake there is a populous area known as Bonne Bay. The people there at the moment do not have the services of electricity. I hope 79951-0-378

they will shortly. In view of the fact that television broadcasting can be given to these people in time, I hope that when the television station at Corner Brook is being examined to find out what its possibilities are that not only will the possibility of providing programs to Steady Brook and Deer Lake by considered but that consideration will also be given to the Bonne Bay area.
I bring these three points to the attention of the minister. They are important to the people of my area. I know the minister is interested in having the C.B.C. bring its services to as many people as possible and I would hope that he would ask the corporation to investigate the possibility of providing better coverage to the people in the areas I have mentioned.

Mr. Chairman, I, like many hon. members who have preceded me wish to speak about television and radio service in some of the remote areas on the west coast of Vancouver island. I live in an area where there is very little television reception. I was surprised to hear the minister stat that 94 per cent of Canadian homes have Canadian television coverage available. I know that he spoke about A, B and C contours of coverage and I would think that the C contour must be a very limited one because I know that there are many people particularly in the west who do not have proper television coverage available to them.
In my own area there is very little television that reaches the west coast of Vancouver island. It hits the odd spot but in general it is scarcely worth the cost of a television set. I should like to ask through the minister that the C.B.C. make a thorough study of the requirements in that area.
In the Port Alberni area which has a population approaching 20,000 people there is little television coverage. The balance of the west coast of the island, if it receives any television service whatever, receives it from United States stations. In Courtenay on the east coast of the island I understand the C.B.C. plan to erect a satellite station on the mountain named Jap Mountain near Cumberland. I also heard that there is some problem here, about a licence for the station because of wave lengths. I trust that this will not delay the installation of this station because it is urgently needed.
It was pointed out to me by a resident of the northern end of the island a few months ago that there is a United States communications cable that goes up Vancouver island and right by their door step at Port Hardy en route to Alaska carrying television communications. They were inquiring about how they might tap into this. If the minister has

Supply-C.B.C.
any ideas on the subject I should like to have them to pass on. It seems strange to these people that such a cable should go by their door step en route to an area that has only slightly more population, if indeed it is as large, than the area of which I am speaking. I hope that the C.B.C. will take the advice that has been offered by previous speakers and first endeavour to bring television to those areas where it means so much, where they have no picture shows, where the people cannot get into a car and drive down the highway to the next town. In fact, many of them are isolated miles apart from any other family.
I trust the corporation will make every effort possible to bring these people the service they so badly need. At one time radio was a great consolation to the people in isolated areas but radio programs have deteriorated to such an extent now that in many cases they are hardly worth listening to. On the northern coast of British Columbia and in the northern part of Vancouver island we do not even have satisfactory radio reception from CBR in Vancouver. In this case again most of the radio reception comes from United States stations. I would ask the C.B.C. through the minister to take a very serious look at this area that is being indoctrinated by foreign propaganda.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments in which to bring before the minister and through him to the C.B.C. the claims of my constituents for improved service. We have heard that the C.B.C. has applied for a permit and is prepared to spend money to provide a television station at Edmonton which already is supplied with service from a private station. It seems to me a warped sense of service is displayed when the C.B.C. is prepared to do this and at the same time to ignore repeatedly year after year-* it has been done-the requests from other places, not for a television service but for a radio service.
My riding contains approximately 50,000 people, and not more than one quarter of them are served by C.B.C. radio. We have asked repeatedly for a small satellite-
Will the hon. member say what stations do serve the constituency?
There is no station that serves my constituency completely.
Does Sydney come in?

Sydney comes in at the western section but only around the Port aux Basques area; from Port aux Basques down as far as Marystown there is a wide gap which receives

hardly any service at all; the service it does receive comes from a private station rather than from the C.B.C.
Where?

Station CJON at St. John's.
The minister mentioned the C.B.C. station at Sydney. That is not a satisfactory station for our needs because my constituents do not rely on a station merely for entertainment. Most of my constituents are fishermen and their interests are tied up with those of our own province. They want to receive weather and market reports; they want to know what has gone on in the capital and it should be one of the prime functions of the C.B.C. to bind us together, to bind Canada together as a nation and certainly to bind the individual parts of a province together. In my riding the C.B.C. is completely failing in that respect.
I am not at all certain that the C.B.C. should be permitted to spend more funds in expanding services or duplicating services in areas which are already served. There is no handicap in being served by a private station. I think it can be proved that in most instances a private station can give better service at much less cost than can the C.B.C. I know in my own province, before we had the microwave linkup, we got excellent programs from station CJON. I know their outlay in giving the service was far less than what the C.B.C. would estimate to provide similar service. I have had an opportunity to compare the programs, when we would be in St. John's, Newfoundland for a number of months and we would get used to seeing the programs over the private station. Then we would come to Ottawa where we would be fed by the C.B.C., and the contrast was certainly unfavourable to the C.B.C. It is true that now the microwave provides us with a sort of instantaneous hookup. We can see events as they happen, but that is only a minor detail because in a vast country like Canada there is the time element and we cannot all look at the same things at the time they happen because the difference in time will not permit it.
While I am talking about the private stations I want to pay tribute to the work they are doing in my province, and in particular to station CJON, both the radio and the television station, and with respect to one of the prime justifications for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, namely that it should be an outlet to provide opportunities for the development of local talent. I want to tell this committee that the private station is doing a much better job in my province in providing for the development of local talent

than I have seen the C.B.C. do in any other part of Canada that I have visited.
As I said before, it seems to me that the C.B.C. has a wonderful opportunity to help give Canada a sense of nationhood; it could make us better known to each other; it could emphasize the principles and values which bind us together as a nation and which must be strengthened if we are to survive. I for one am concerned about the extent to which the C.B.C., by their programs is in many ways undermining and weakening those very values. I think the security of Canada as a nation is better protected by the private stations than by the C.B.C.
As 1 said before, the provision of a satellite would not be very expensive. The private station was able to provide one and I do not see why the C.B.C. cannot provide a small satellite to fill the gap which is not now covered. My colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's, spoke about the station in Corner Brook. Port aux Basques is only a short distance from Corner Brook and yet it cannot receive the programs. I believe a small satellite either at Port aux Basques or Grand Bank would overcome any difficulty. The least we can do is to have somebody investigate this and make certain before the C.B.C. starts spending money to duplicate services already in existence.
I wish to make one more point before I sit down. The idea came to me while I was listening to my colleague from Humber-St. George's refer to the station at Harmon Field. We do not have any television coverage to speak of. If there are 100 families in my riding who are able to receive television programs that would be the outside number. Television is not a big issue with the majority of my constituents because they have not the means to buy a television set even if the service were available. I was wondering whether it may not be possible to serve the more densely populated area around Port aux Basques from Harmon Field? I should like the minister to follow up the idea and see whether some arrangements can be made with the United States authorities there so that the station might be given more power and extend its coverage to at least the Port aux Basques area.

Mr. Chairman, we are called upon today to approve the estimates of the C.B.C., which amount to about $71 million, i.e. $4 per head for each Canadian citizen. In consequence, for the large families I represent and who live in my constituency, where there are generally from 6 to 7 children to a family-which means a family of 8 persons-the contribution amounts to about $100 a year for helping the government create something we have no means of controlling. On the whole, all we are asked to do today, is to pass phantom estimates. Because, if I scan the blue book and come to page 11, I am referred for further details to page 128. I therefore look up page 128, but I am no wiser because there on the page where the details are explained I see there is a $62 million grant, and, at the second paragraph another grant of $7 million.
On the other hand, a little further on complete details are given respecting the administration of the international shortwave broadcasting service.
I do not understand why there is such a big difference between what must be kept secret in this corporation's administration and what is willingly revealed as far as the shortwave division is concerned.
At the outset of my remarks, I wish to acknowledge the presence of Mr. Ouimet. I hope that his recent gall bladder operation was successful and that he is now fully recovered and in a position to carry out his usual duties.
I know that, before his operation, Mr. Ouimet may not have been able to withstand certain pressures in his service, even from highly placed officials. That is why I am glad to note that he is well again and I urge him to direct with a firm hand the internal administration of the corporation.
Referring once again to the blue book, I wish to consider the estimates of various departments.
Under agriculture, for instance, the appropriations for this year are about $41.6 million. As for the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the amount is $59.3 million. Under the Department of Defence Production, estimates total $23 million; for external affairs, estimates reach about $83 million. Therefore, I am inclined to compare

Supply-C.B.C.
those figures with the C.B.C. estimates and I find that no others impose a heavier burden on the national economy. That is why members of this house are anxious to obtain fuller information respecting the internal administration of the C.B.C. and to learn especially for what purpose the moneys voted to the corporation every year are actually used.
Mr. Chairman, I think this is the reason why some members had strong but sound criticisms to voice against the estimates we are called upon to pass today. I therefore urge the minister to investigate more closely those responsible for C.B.C. administration because I suggest that he will discover flaws in the administrative structure of the organization. To give only one example, may I point out that I suggested a few months ago that the C.B.C. should consider building its new offices in Montreal's east end. I therefore wrote to several people, among others to Mr. Gerard Lamarche, French director general of the C.B.C. for the province of Quebec, to Mr. Ouimet and to the minister. I also wrote to Montreal municipal authorities.
In his letter to me, Mr. Lamarche said the responsibility for the establishing of offices in any place is not his, but rather that of the authorities of the city of Montreal.
The minister, on the other hand, told me to inquire from the C.B.C.
I wrote to the regional director who also told me to inquire from the authorities of the city of Montreal. Later, he came back on his advice and told me to inquire from the chairman of the C.B.C.
The C.B.C.'s plan to establish its offices in the eastern section of Montreal is commendable, and I am quite happy to see that some of those offices are to be built in the constituency of St. Mary, that I have the honour to represent.
Those offices could be built at Repentigny if the city of Montreal does not want them.

Mr. Chairman, after reading the letter which a senior official of the C.B.C. addressed to me, I am led to believe that the corporation lacked objectivity in the choice of that site, because I had sent them a very definite plan, in which the land, the topography and the esthetic of the place had been considered. A serious study of my suggested alternative was, I think, rejected. Yet sev-

eral thousands of dollars were spent in investigating the project which the corporation has now under study, whereas the document I have here at hand cost absolutely nothing, either to the C.B.C., or to the city of Montreal, or to the province of Quebec.
Anyway, as I say, I am happy to find that the C.B.C., together with the authorities of the city of Montreal, agreed to build its offices in a part of my riding. Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twistingate-Twillingate (Mr. Pick-ersgill) stated this morning that on second reading of the bill of rights we agreed last night that the Liberals had a right to be admitted to the C.B.C., like everybody else. If that is not a shameful and disgusting situation, I wonder what our Liberal friends will call it. And if a royal commission is appointed, I shall submit the name of that person.

Mr. Chairman, I should also like to call the attention of the house to the poor organization of the film purchasing department in the C.B.C. As you will realize, we have to go by the information supplied to us, because there is no information in the estimates and we have to take what we get from outside. It is that attitude that is causing dissatisfaction and turning public opinion against the C.B.C.
For instance, I should like to mention the case of a person who called on the C.B.C. with a film made at Ste Anne de Beaupre. It was a documentary, and the person had really made a masterpiece out of it. This person called on a certain authority in the C.B.C. and was told this: "If you wish to sell your film, you must see Mr. X, and if Mr. X is willing, well, we shall buy it." If my friends in the opposition wish to know the names, I shall give some to them.
Mr. Chairman, this is an unfortunate situation. In my opinion it is an abuse that has been going on for too long in the C.B.C. The trouble is that parliament has no control over the corporation's expenditures. In fact, the C.B.C. paid prohibitive prices for certain films which could have been bought for half, if not a third of the price.
Why? Because there is no control whatsoever by the elected members of this house.
I would like to raise another point to show to what extent there is interference and maladministration in the corporation, merely because the Canadian parliament has no control over C.B.C. finances.
Some time ago, an air conditioning system was to be installed in the corporation building. Experts from companies specializing in this field were called upon and the installation of the system was requested. According to the experts, who sent me a report, the system was put in at a cost of $9,000; it was an air unit which is called air eliminator.
Technically, the system was rated as a 5 power unit. That equipment could therefore have been bought for $6,500. Moreover, Mr. Chairman, some engineers told me that the installed unit was inadequate for its intended purpose.
That is what we deplore, in this house- that lack of control by parliament.
I think our friends in the opposition are as anxious as we are to look through and

Supply-C.B.C.
investigate the expenses of the C.B.C., to determine whether the money has been spent honestly and usefully.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to come back to a point I had stressed a few moments ago. I mean the patronage which prevails in the award of jobs in the C.B.C. The situation is similar to that in the civil service commission. When anybody wants a position for a friend, an examination is announced and the candidate is notified of the competition. Soon after it has been announced, the posters are quickly removed, obviously for the purpose of eliminating competition, while-though only ostensibly-conforming with the requirements of decency.
I have here a statement by somebody who told me he was interested in a position as departmental clerk. The competition announcement was posted on August 20, 1957 in the St. Luc street building, but the staff which might have been interested in this job was working on Dorchester street. Obviously, the very fact points to a desire to avert the attention of those who might have been interested in this job. Of course the person I am referring to did not get the job.
There is another fact I would like to mention. A vacancy was advertised in the stagehand section, which was, in fact, looking for a scenery shifter.
Now, Mr. Chairman, those things are current practice in the C.B.C.
I have here a list of people employed by the corporation. I see here the names of two brothers, and then those of two brothers-in-law.
A strange thing that happened, and it obviously happened before the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) was elected, is that as I notice, the score of people on that list all come from St. Hyacinthe. They were, without any doubt, recommended by the former administration. Do you not find this a rather strange coincidence?
Claude Fontaine, Rosaire Fontaine-

Our friends in the opposition seem to relish the situation. It is indeed, very funny that there should be political patronage in the C.B.C., but they are the ones who introduced it ever since the C.B.C. was first established in this country.
If a certain hon. member would not mind toning down his voice, I shall add that not long ago, a fairly high level job was secured in the C.B.C. thanks to a letter of recommendation signed by a member of the opposition.

Before raising cries of patronage or unwarranted interference, hon. members opposite should look at themselves and go through their files.
It is like the C.N.R.
Never mind the C.N.R., stick to the C.B.C.
A member rose and talked about leftism.
Grignon.

I am accused of making unfounded charges.
Now here is something from a newspaper which I never read, but which was sent to me. The name of this paper is Vers Demain. On page 6 of the May 15, 1958 issue, I find the following-
Mr. Chairman, I would ask you to call our friends in the opposition to order. If they want to make speeches, let them make them in due time; however, I hope they will make more sense than the speech made by the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis).
It hurt you.

No, it hurt you. I shall now quote from page 6 of the newspaper in question:
The C.B.C. has become a socialist stronghold, and they know it. That is why they fear anything that threatens to take it away from them. On June 10 last year, whenever election reports showed Conservative gains and Liberal losses, the faces of Rene Levesque and Andre Laurendeau took on a gloomy expression. And before the elections of March 31 last, expecting the Conservative party to strengthen its position in Ottawa, the socialist weekly Vrai forecast in large headlines that the antisocialists (he called them Duplessists) were preparing to oust the archangels of Canadian socialism from the C.B.C.
Further down in the same article, reference is made to Jacques Hebert, publisher of that sheet dealing with the scandal at Bordeaux.
Jacques Hebert wrote that before the March 31 elections, when, expecting the final victory of the Conservatives, he already had his handkerchief out to cry at the expected departure of his friends and himself from "the last oasis of freedom, the national film board and the C.B.C., where the air is still breathable" (breathable for them, of course).
I go on quoting from the same article which mentions Jacques Hebert, that friend of hon. members in the opposition.
People of talent, such as Andre Laurendeau, will have to give way to idiotic nobodies-Every leftist will be thrown out: Pierre-Elliot Trudeau, Gerard Pelletier, Fernand Seguin, Jean-Louis Gagnon, etc. -It will be a triumph for stupidity when the only thinking men have been eliminated from the C.B.C.-

You would think anyone who is not a Liberal is an idiot.
Every leftist will be thrown out of the C.B.C.
Those are not my words, they are in the article.
It will be a triumph for stupidity when the only thinking men have been eliminated from the C.B.C.
Those are not my words, they are the words of the leftists, people on the payroll of our friends in the opposition.
Mr. Chairman, I am not here to indulge in petty politics. I submit to the house that I do not stoop, like certain members on my right, to the point of making comments on municipal, provincial or federal elections.
I was not elected here to indulge in petty politics.
If our friends here were as conscious of it as we are, they would try to fulfil the pledges they gave their fellow citizens.
In my opinion, it is the duty of any member who is conscious of his obligations to rise and protest strongly against certain institutions or crown corporations which abuse their powers.
We are asked to vote $71 million, without even being told what that money will be used for. It is for that reason that I join with my friends who spoke before me, to demand a royal inquiry into the business of the C.B.C., in order that the people themselves, those who have any grievances against the C.B.C., may have the opportunity of expressing their views on this matter.
I should like to quote here from an article published in Montreal Matin of February 11, 1959, reproduced from he Bien Public of Three Rivers:
Parliament, which is responsible to the people, has the duty to examine the present establishment of the C.B.C. and to apply the necessary reforms. Let our leaders hasten to shed some light on the C.B.C., whose internal chaos has just been revealed to the public by the strike. A body which has absorbed half a billion dollars since its creation must not escape examination.
I close my remarks by asking you to draw the minister's attention to the fact that we cannot ask the people of Canada to spend $71 million inconsiderately without knowing what that money will be used for. I would call upon our friends opposite, who are so talkative from their seats-having but nonsense to talk about, and who take the floor on government measures always in such a way as to break the rules-who insult their opponents rather than state the facts, to pronounce themselves honestly on that matter and to stop resorting to patronage with the C.B.C.
Not long ago, Mr. Chairman, I entertained at my home a former Liberal party organizer
Supply-C.B.C.
who told me that wrestlers' mattresses had been ordered for a C.B.C. program. When he sent in his bill, it was returned with the remark: "You are not very wise to charge only that amount, send another bill and charge three times as much."
Well, Mr. Chairman, that is exactly so, that is exactly the kind of expenditures that we do not want to accept in the House of Commons. That is why we want to know where the money goes, and how it is being spent.
Are you going to vote for or against?

What are you going to do yourself?

When this battle in Quebec is finished, Mr. Chairman, I will commence. I rise particularly to deal with one or two matters of particular concern to my constituents. However, before going into the details I must on behalf of this party emphasize the fact that this party wholeheartedly supports the C.B.C. as a necessary institution in Canadian life. Like any other organization, whether it is public or private, it may on occasion suffer from administrative indigestion or growing pains. However, I am quite sure that many of the things that have been complained about today will be soon corrected if necessary-as they usually are corrected-in the proper way and in time.
We in this group believe that it is a healthy and proper state of affairs if we have the C.B.C. as a public corporation and the private radio interests in this country competing together on a proper basis. We think the net result of that state of affairs will be to the advantage of the Canadian people.
I should also explain that while the hon. member for Port Arthur mentioned that in his view the educated elite live in the large centres-and that may be true-I am speaking on behalf of the cultured country people of Kootenay West. I would not mind saying that if you wanted to assess the educational standards in the small city of Trail and district you would find a larger percentage of people in that city and district with university degrees than are to be found possibly in most other areas in Canada. I also want to mention the fact that I represent vigorous frontier-minded people who have not lost their vigour or their willingness to live pioneer lives.
My people make their own entertainment on an exceptional scale. As far as the stage

Supply-C.B.C.
is concerned they are served by little theatre groups. As far as music is concerned they have their own bands and small orchestras. As far as sports are concerned they have baseball, hockey, curling, track and field sports, water sports, fishing and hunting. They are all indulged in and I mention them to bring to the attention of the committee that I represent a cultured and vigorous people who still evidence their pioneering instincts in many fields. They also appreciate the C.B.C. as a Canadian institution. Generally speaking you find an appreciation of the C.B.C. services across Canada. When it comes to entertainment you find people who prefer one program to another, but I think it is fair to say that the bulk of Canadians are proud of and support the general policies and activities of the C.B.C.
I have been very interested when travelling in the United States, in the states of Washington, Idaho, Montana and New York to find out what a high opinion many people in the United States have of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and its programs. In this connection I wish to quote briefly from an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal entitled "Not without honour". In part it says:
Witness the comment of Mr. Jack Gould of the New York Times on that favorite target, the C.B.C.:
"Discriminating Americans close to the border ... repeatedly have apprised the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that its radio network is a veritable model of civilized behavior on the airwaves. It is."
To support the view that "Canadian radio can stand comparison with the best aural efforts of any nation", Mr. Gould points out that "Canadians are firmly convinced that live classical music on the radio is not only a joy to the ear but also a cultural resource to be preserved", and praises our "substantial radio drama, which has practically become extinct in the United States".
I am getting very close to the problems of my own people. It is because of the interest of the people I represent in good music, in good commentaries and in the cultural things the C.B.C. provides that those who are denied them today are anxious to receive them at the first opportunity.
Now a word about the television satellite to be erected to serve the Rossland-Trail area. All I say in that connection is that it has been delayed for over a year by certain difficulties in connection with the leasing of a site on the mountain behind Rossland but the people in the area are looking forward to the commencement of the operation of that station. As a result of the construction of this station a satellite will be erected somewhere behind the Beasley bluffs to serve the Nelson area, and I would like to bring to the minister's attention the fact that some

apprehension is felt that although the satellite is welcomed by the great majority of the people it will not serve a good number of the people it is intended to serve.
In that connection may I quote briefly from the Nelson News of June 8, 1960:
-Grade A service will be provided from the local satellite to Nelson, Crescent Valley, South Slocan, Bonnington Falls, Shoreacres and surrounding rural area, and grade B service to Tarrys, Thrums, Robson, Castlegar, Brilliant, Blueberry Creek, Kinnaird and a larger rural area.
The station will operate on channel 9.
Nelson authorities who have studied contour maps and consulted other data, doubt that the signal will cover lower Fairview or the north shore unless some unknown freak condition exists or some mechanical provision is made.
They said that Nelson mountain's 3000-foot elevation would likely block reception to these areas.
CBC-TV is expected to reach Nelson this winter.
I was informed later by letter that these contours and maps were drawn by engineers in the district who have experience in radio and television and they are very concerned that the district of Fairview, which is almost half the city of Nelson, and the north shore which represents a relatively closely settled area on the north shore of the north arm of Kootenay lake will not be serviced by the proposed satellite station. I would urge that the C.B.C. give serious consideration to this fear before erecting this television satellite. I think it is a good idea these things should be checked up very carefully, especially in a mountainous region such as the Kootenays where there is such difficulty in getting signals in many cases from even a short distance.
Now I come to a matter I have mentioned before and I am sure the minister is not surprised to hear me mention it again. It concerns the two or three low power relay radio transmitters which are required to service the 3,000 or 4,000 people still denied radio service in Kootenay West. It concerns an area in the Upper Arrow lake which should be served by a low power relay transmitter in Nakusp and one required in the Balfour-Procter area to serve the area around those villages and the surrounding shores of Kootenay lake. I am receiving constant complaints about lack of radio in this area. It was expected at one time that the Balfour-Procter area would be served by an increase in the power of the station at Nelson, but unfortunately these expectations have not been fulfilled and these people are still denied radio reception.
A great number of people are interested in television, but I have noticed how many people in my constituency are fond of listening to the radio. In fact I think radio is making a recovery. I find that many people

who have had televisior for some time tell me they enjoy listening to radio programs and radio speeches more than they do to television. The people I am speaking about in the smaller areas who want to get the low power relay transmitters and the television service want them because they are a cultured informed people who want the programs of the C.B.C.
In connection with the recovery of radio I will quote very briefly from the Canadian Commentator of December, 1959, which supports my own experience in the constituency which I have the honour to represent:
The Fowler commission proved that radio is anything but a secondary form of home entertainment, where people want news and informed comment they go-of necessity-to radio. They are buying more sets than they ever did before and it's not unusual now to find people who can tell you what was on radio the previous evening. A hopeful sign.
People are re-discovering the pleasure of listening to good music (completely absent on the "other medium"), the stimulation of intelligent debate: they are discovering that they have an imagination, and this because the radio play demands attention and the use of the mind.
They are beginning to forget the horror of quiz shows, performing seals and thundering horses.
Radio has come home-to stay.
I think there is a great deal in what is said in that paragraph. It is because of this interest in radio that I make a final appeal -I hope it is a final appeal-to the minister and the officials of the C.B.C. for low power relay transmitters at Nakusp to serve the Upper Arrow lakes where some 3,000 people have been denied satisfactory radio reception to date.
A similar situation exists in the Balfour-Procter district. Nakusp is the headquarters in the area for sawmills and lumbering activities generally. The population is engaged in producing forest and agricultural products. All through the years to date they have been seeking an opportunity to hear the C.B.C. It is possible to get the Trail, Kamloops and Kelowna stations in the daytime under certain conditions but there has been no opportunity to listen to the C.B.C. on a dependable basis.
In the Arrow lakes area there are approximately 3,000 people who are still thus denied radio reception and the opportunity to listen to the C.B.C. They are also denied television reception. Lately they have had some experimental television service by the use of a gadget put on top of Saddle mountain but I understand they can only receive signals from Spokane. Many people ask me how soon they can expect the opportunity to hear and see C.B.C. programs. These people are anxious to receive C.B.C. radio and television reception. They wish to enjoy its cultural and other programs.
Supply-C.B.C.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to support the hon. member for Kootenay West in his plea to the department for the establishment of radio and television services in isolated areas. I do not go along with him in the doctrine that the government should continue with the C.B.C. I believe that the sooner we turn it over to private interests the better off we will be.
I noticed recently an article in the press stating that many millions of dollars will be spent in the area of Montreal this year for C.B.C. buildings and equipment. If some of this money were spread around in the small rural districts of Canada in providing radio and television service it would be of vast assistance. I do not believe that all C.B.C. expenditures should be localized in the larger centres.
I wish to point out the need for improved service in Kootenay East which borders on Kootenay West as was mentioned by the previous speaker. As the hon. gentleman said there are certain localities in this area where no radio reception is possible. We are situated in the midst of the Rocky mountains and because the valleys are not very wide our reception is subject to serious interference. Long before this government came into power requests were made of the federal administration to establish a booster station in the lake Windermere valley which is noted all over the world for its radium hot springs. It enjoys a considerable tourist trade and some consideration should be given to the establishment of radio reception facilities so that tourists and the local residents may enjoy C.B.C. programs. No reception exists at present. We are dependent on a small local station which is unable to give us the service we require. The cost of establishing small booster stations would not be very great especially in this area and I know the local residents who have a keen interest in the matter would greatly appreciate some consideration being shown to the establishment of booster stations.
I wish now to direct my attention to the question of television reception. Companies have come into the area and piped television reception into the cities and towns but the people in rural areas are still denied C.B.C. television reception. I believe the time has come when we must begin to meet the needs of the people living in the outlying areas of Canada who are just as entitled as those in the larger centres to television service. I realize it is difficult to provide reception to rural areas but this could be done by the establishment of small satellite stations by which means C.B.C. television programs could be brought into the area.

Supply-C.B.C.
In view of the plans that have been made for the expenditure of many millions of dollars in the larger centres I urge the minister and his department to consider spending some of this money to establish satellite stations in small rural areas and to improve radio reception there so that those living in isolated communities, our farmers and those in logging and mining camps can enjoy the advantages of this service. This service would make their lives more enjoyable. We have a limited range of reception at present in the outlying areas of Kootenay East in the Rocky mountains.
Would the hon. member say exactly what area it is of which he is speaking?

I am referring to the Kootenay East district and the lake Windermere valley and all the territory in the Kootenay East section. If many millions of dollars can be spent by the C.B.C. in the Montreal area this year I feel some of this money could be spread around among smaller communities to give our Canadian people better service than they are now receiving.
