Mr. Chairman, I have only a few brief remarks to make about the speeches which have been made since this morning by the hon. members for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay), for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), for St. Mary (Mr. Valade) and for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon), who made several unfounded charges against the C.B.C.
I refer to some of the charges made by the member for Roberval who claims that the C.B.C. refuses to reveal how it is spending the money it gets from parliament. As he said, they do what they like with it. The member for Roberval added that the C.B.C. gives insolent answers to the questions asked by the representatives of the people. Besides, he said that the C.B.C. is a hot bed of favouritism and political patronage.
The member for Berthier-Maskinonge-De-lanaudiere calls it a corporation where public funds are squandered.
The member for St. Mary talks about a ghost budget, about a family compact, about favoritism in employment and maladministration in the purchase of films.
I would not want for a moment to question the right of any member of this house to ask questions and demand answers. This is the reason why we are here. But this morning, following the speech of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, I rose to ask him this very simple question:

The time has come, the occasion is perfect, if you have questions to ask or specific charges to make, please make them right now to the minister and his officials. I must add that the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm backed out and that he did not follow up my question.
Mr. Chairman, the hon. members did not make a single specific charge, did not state any specific fact, no name or date, and I have much sympathy for the Minister of National Revenue who, with the officials of his department, has been indirectly flaunted. But he should not be surprised, since the Conservative members who acted this way have recently lost a patronage monopoly which they valued very much and we think they would want to regain here certain benefits they have lost in the province of Quebec.
In any event, for the last two years, the Conservative members, and the member for Roberval in particular, have been witchhunting about the C.B.C., just like a certain American representative from Wisconsin who certainly did not render his country all the services he could.
I believe that the general public, especially in the province of Quebec, because I am more familiar with the facts there than in other provinces, trusts the C.B.C. and its administrators.
I have often heard those hon. members strongly criticizing some programs but it is strange that those very members, to my knowledge, never managed to commend the fine productions and activities of the C.B.C.
When one wishes to be fair and give credit to everybody, one must take into consideration the good things as well as the bad ones. And if this is done judiciously and conscientiously, I say that we may be proud of the C.B.C., of its performers, of its productions that are just as good as foreign productions, taking into account the funds available.
I leave it to the minister to deal with the accusations made by those hon. members. He knows them much better than I do and he must know whether there are motives that prompt such remarks and, if any, what they are.
As far as I am concerned, I believe that if an organization needs the trust of parliament and the public, it is indeed the C.B.C. which has a duty so complex, so important and so difiicult to perform for the Canadian people. So long as we shall hear vague and irresponsible statements such as those we have heard, I shall continue to rely on the corporation.

In conclusion, may I give this friendly advice to the minister? When he took over this important department which reports for the C.B.C., he was taking over from men who had kept the C.B.C. free from political influence. Moreover, if the minister keeps on the course we have set for him, he will have rendered a great service to his country by holding firm against pressures exerted by his friends.
(Text):

I wonder whether the minister would say a few words with regard to the over-all policy of the C.B.C. in servicing all rural areas, not just those of Kootenay East or Kootenay West?
Of course, the reason for establishing the C.B.C., as I understand it, was to disseminate Canadian culture to all Canadian people, and there was no suggestion that it should be given to urban people rather than to rural people. I represent a constituency which is almost wholly rural and in some of our areas, on account of geographical conditions, it is impossible to be serviced by a privately owned station; it is not economically sound to do so. But those people have contributed toward the $69 million, as have other people, and I am quite sure it was the intention of the government that they should receive benefits as do all other Canadians.
I should like to know whether there is a policy and whether it is taken step by step? It is quite reasonable to believe that the more densely populated areas of the urban regions should be serviced first, but there should be a definite policy that all hon. members could take home to their constituents, particularly those representing rural areas.

First of all, I should like to agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in one respect. I refer to what he had to say about many suggestions made by some of our Quebec Tory members today. As he said, I can disagree violently with what they say, but also I would stand very firm on their freedom to say it, for this reason. How can I judge what they have to say if I do not give them a chance to say it? Only by giving them the opportunity to say it can you know how much you are against that type of thing.
But the hon. member went further in his remarks. He pointed out something that is the very crux of many of the problems and of the criticisms of the C.B.C. I do not think I can recall word for word what he said but certainly, as I understood him, his remarks
Supply-C.B.C.
were to the effect that he had always supported the C.B.C., not because it was a publicly owned system but because Canada could not remain a separate country without public broadcasting. This is quite an admission because it means that if we had to rely on private broadcasting we would not even have a country. According to the words of the hon. member, it would be impossible to have a country if we had to depend on private enterprise; but he is against public enterprise even though it is impossible to have a country without it.

I am sure the hon. gentleman does not want to be unfair. I did not say I was against public enterprise or for public enterprise. I said I did not support the C.B.C. because it was public enterprise but because, in my opinion, it was necessary for the preservation of Canada.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that is exactly what I just said.
No, not at all.

I do not think it is any reflection upon the hon. member. I think he has just expressed the confusion we have in our society in Canada today. He has expressed the sense of confusion that we have. It seems we want to have our cake and eat it, too.
The C.B.C. was started as a public service to supply broadcasting services to people across this country where private enterprise could not or would not supply the service. As soon as we set up this public service we started to criticize it. Why? Because it cost us money. How we can supply a service without costing money is something that nobody has ever explained to me yet. The one thing I do not like about this whole situation is the way in which we continue to delude ourselves that we can get free service from private broadcasting.
We have fooled ourselves and fooled the people of Canada generally in believing that private broadcasting stations supply free entertainment. Where do they get the money with which to supply the free entertainment they provide? Is it not out of the very same pocket from which the government has to collect taxes to support the C.B.C.? I do not know from what other source the money could be obtained. The matter boils down to the fact that if we want to supply a broadcasting service across this country we have to pay for it. The hon. member for Kootenay East advocated that we sell the whole thing to private enterprise but I shudder to think what that would do to the broadcasting service in this country or even in Kootenay East which the hon. member represents.

Supply-C.B.C.
It puts me in mind of a situation we often see in communities. A householder will become so incensed at his tax bill that he will get rid of his property and move to the country or to the outskirts of the community, but as soon as he gets there he immediately demands the same services he had when in town and by the time he gets them his taxes are back at the same level they were in the first place. The situation is like a man wrestling with his conscience. We want all the benefits of socialism as long as we do not call them socialism. We want to get rid of all the evils of our so-called free enterprise system and at the same time still maintain it.
Order.

I do not know where that interjection came from. I think we must clear our thinking on this matter and endeavour to put a stop to the selfdelusion that is prevalent in this country. Conservative members from the province of Quebec have criticized the C.B.C. very severely today, mainly on two grounds. The first is the fact that the C.B.C. has permitted people to appear on its programs who disagree with these members politically and the other has to do with the terrible cost hanging around the necks of the taxpayers.
I think we have to realize once and for all that if we are going to supply service through the C.B.C.-many hon. members from widely scattered areas have complained bitterly that the C.B.C. does not supply the service it should in some areas-we have got to pay for the service. We must keep in mind that if we are not going to put the C.B.C. on a straight public service basis with its expenses paid out of general revenue then we must at least give it an opportunity to get into some of the lucrative fields which in far too many cases are reserved for private broadcasting.
We seem to have the idea in this country that if there is a profit to be made out of anything private enterprise should get it but if it is a matter of providing a straight service which will impose a burden it should be done by public enterprise. Yet as soon as that is done there are complaints about the cost of the public enterprise. In my opinion this is one of the problems that the minister, the officials of the C.B.C. and the people of Canada as a whole should face up to.
I have mentioned on previous occasions that the favourite pastime of the Canadian people seems to be to fool themselves that as long as the cost of something is hidden it is free, but once we look into the matter we run into the unalterable fact that there is nothing free. Such services are paid for either directly

or indirectly, and I think we should make up our minds just what we want to do with public broadcasting. Do we want it to do a job as a public service? Do we want it made available to as many Canadians as possible, if not all, or do we want it to be castigated and criticized as it has been today, this way, that way and the other way?
I am sure we do not mind criticism of the C.B.C. provided it is justifiable and constructive criticism put forward with the idea of improving the service now given, but I certainly hope that before the minister and the government listens to the recommendation of the hon. member for Kootenay East, which I noticed was also applauded by other members, and takes such a step it will look ahead a bit and see what the consequences will be.

Mr. Chairman, I am not rising to make a speech but merely to correct a misrepresentation. I do not accuse the hon. member for Timmins of doing so intentionally but I think he misrepresented my position somewhat and I should like to make it very clear. I said or intended to say and thought I had said that I did not support the C.B.C. because it was a public corporation rather than a private corporation but that I supported the C.B.C. and public broadcasting because I thought it was essential to the maintenance of this country as a separate country, and I think it is.
But in saying that I had no intention of suggesting that most of the private broadcasters in this country, though there are a few I do not admire very much, do not have a very high sense of public service. But they are local in character and in nature and this country extends over 5,000 miles, and if we are to have any Canadian broadcasting at all it is beyond the capacity of anyone who has to put up his own money in a corporation to establish the kind of national networks that I believe are necessary to keep this country Canadian. That is the point I was seeking to make.
I think it is a very fortunate thing that we never did go whole hog as Mr. Bennett intended we should go at the time the Canadian radio commission was established in 1932 and nationalize all broadcasting. Looking back, I think it is a very good thing that we have the C.B.C. and I think it is a very good thing that we have private broadcasting, but as long as we have this situation there is going to be a difficult area in between, as the hon. member so justly said. I did not want anyone to represent me as taking the view that private broadcasters are not just as capable of being patriotic and good Canadians as public broadcasters.

Mr. Chairman, I would merely ask the minister to try to improve the television service in the upper part of Gatineau constituency.
The chambers of commerce of my constituency and of neighbouring constituencies like those of Pontiac and Labelle, as well as the union of chambers of commerce of western Quebec, have asked for the setting up of a satellite station on Mount Ryan, near lake Ste. Marie.
I know that the C.B.C. has considered that request, and I know that it is sympathetic to it, because such an improvement would benefit a population of 40,000 inhabitants in the Mont Laurier area, in the northern area of the Lievre, and the northern area of the Gatineau as well as in part of Pontiac constituency.
At the present time, reception at Maniwaki, which is about 80 miles from Ottawa, is sometimes very good, and we may say that, in general, it is average and even acceptable, because there is a private community station there. Those who are served by that station, must first pay a $100 fee to connect their television set to the main cable, and afterwards they must pay $36 a year. I think that the same situation prevails in Mont Laurier.
According to information available to me, the erection of a satellite tower on Ryan mountain would improve the service in the whole area. I therefore ask the minister to look favourably on this request made by the chambers of commerce of this area and of neighbouring ridings.

I would like, at the outset, to apologize for taking the time of the house. If it were not for a certain challenge from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) I would have been satisfied with leaving it to my colleagues from Ber-thier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) and Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) to express certain views that I share with them.
I would like also to take this opportunity to congratulate the new leader of the opposition, the suave member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) and his assistant the waggish member for St. Denis (Mr. Denis). I say that, after so many years, the Liberal party finally allows them to express their opinions. It remains to be seen whether the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate should be transferred to the back benches and henceforth take his lead from the members for Maisonneuve-Rosemont and for St. Denis. But it is not for me to decide. The Leader of the Opposition will regret it or will
Supply-C.B.C.
congratulate himself after the next election, unless he puts an end to this thing as early as Monday morning next, or at five o'clock tonight, at the latest.
However, I will not pursue the matter unduly, as I just want to discuss-as I and my colleagues are entitled to-the funds the house is now being asked to vote for the operations of the C.B.C.
One thing that strikes me, Mr. Chairman, is that when the estimates of certain departments come before the house, some members on the government side rise to voice certain criticisms, particularly against the C.B.C. That is their right, it is even a duty. I think the people will be the first to commend them for it, because they display an independent mind and make no bones about revealing anything wrong in some division or other of the federal administration.
It is the very essence of a democratic party. I for one am sure that the people of the province of Quebec and especially the citizens of the Chambly-Rouville riding will bear me out on that point. As for me, I congratulate my colleagues on being brave and dutiful enough to criticize the administration of a department even though their own party is in office.
It is the basis of democracy and I fail to see why the hon. members of the opposition criticize such a stand.
Ironically, every time a member on the government side criticizes or ventures to make the slightest unkind remark concerning the C.B.C., its administration, the acts of its officers or of some of its employees, immediately the Liberal members protest sharply against what they call an infringement upon the freedom of speech, the freedom of this, the freedom of that. Well you may be sure that before long we shall hear them lash into the wording of the bill of rights, and if we, Conservative members, venture to exercise our right to speak in order to criticize in any way any department, and more particularly the C.B.C., you will hear them refer to the bill of rights and accuse us of infringing upon the freedom of the C.B.C., of its commentators, of its officers and of its employees.
Mr. Chairman, mention is made of political patronage. I wonder if this would not be the main reason for the stand which the Liberal members have taken, and more particularly the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Mr. Chairman, I would ask you not to be hasty in calling me to order. There has been an election recently in a province. The Liberal members, taking pride in a halfvictory which they keep talking about, continue in this house to nag the party-
5996	HOUSE OF
Supply-C.B.C.
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order; I am afraid I shall have to call the hon. member to order. I think the Chair has been quite lenient, but I shall have to ask the hon. member to come back to vote 41, which is for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
(Translation):

Exactly, Mr. Chairman, I cautioned you against hastiness in calling me to order.
I wanted to say that some hon. members, continuing that election campaign, are apparently riled whenever a Conservative member criticizes the attitude of certain C.B.C. employees or officials. Apparently, that private hunting ground of the Liberal and C.C.F. parties, that socialist and Liberal propaganda mill, is not to be touched. Such an attitude is calculated to give the Canadian people the impression that we are trying to make a political hotbed out of the C.B.C. That is what the people are being led to believe about those who try to voice honest criticisms, as is their right, at the unreasonable and unconstitutional attitude of the C.B.C. when our friends rise in defence of those who, within the C.B.C., work against the purposes of that organization and try to turn it into a political hotbed.
Mr. Chairman, no Conservative member has ever asked or even wanted that the C.B.C. should become a political organization, a propaganda machine in the hands of the government in office. However, Liberal members have denounced our attitude every time one of us demanded that the C.B.C. should no longer be used for political or propaganda purposes in favour of a particular party. This is so true that a moment ago, paradoxically I drew a mirthless smirk from the member for Bonavista-Twillingate when I asked him in the course of his remarks, what political propaganda he was referring to in quoting from some newspaper article.
Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. is an institution which Canadians generally have a right to be proud of. Such an organization is, for Canadians generally, a bulwark against Americanism in Canada. I have nothing against Americans, I have no criticism of their behaviour in any field whatsoever; but Canada is an independent country, and wants to remain independent. Its leaders therefore have a with the historical context, the present day


context and the Canadian and French Canadian context. We have a broadcasting network which I think in principle does contribute to the promotion and development of a Canadian culture, while at the same time respecting and even promoting French culture in Canada.
We think the C.B.C. is to be commended, and its leaders are worthy of the highest compliments as far as principles are concerned. Must we, however, as representatives of the people, blindly vote $71 million without raising questions, without denouncing the wrongs of certain officials or employees of the C.B.C., or of certain profiteers orbiting like satellites around this organization which is the property of the people and should be used for the people?
Ask your questions, now is the time.
Mr. Chairman, the genius is telling me to ask questions-
Go ahead, ask questions.

He is repeating what the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Deschatelets) said this morning.
We have no intention of asking questions of the minister and then be told that he has no power to investigate directly, that he must rely on whatever information C.B.C. officials will see fit to let him have.
We have not got the time today. The hon. member for St. Denis who, after all, has a modicum of intelligence will admit that we have not the time to ask all the questions we would like to. Nor, surely, have we time to bother the minister with those questions. Liberal members-especially the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-refer to the minister as the reporter of the C.B.C., "the minister who reports to parliament for the C.B.C.", showing that, as far as they understand the status of the C.B.C. towards parliament, the C.B.C. enjoys full independence, which allows it to reply to questions, through the minister, as it sees fit.
We have had several examples of replies given to questions asked by members.
The hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Parizeau) asked questions about a certain C.B.C. commentator, who was recently elected to the Quebec legislature.
Liberal members would do well not to applaud too fast, because that commentator

turned representative is already tangled in his electric wires.
In reply to the question asked by the hon. member for Lake St. John, we heard the minister say that it was impossible to reply. I do not blame him, because he was acting within the limits of his functions in accordance with the powers conferred upon him. He could not go any further. He could not force those gentlemen of the C.B.C. to reply to the representative of the people, he who is responsible for the supervision of the C.B.C. That is the deadlock in which we find ourselves every time reference is made to the C.B.C., a body financed by the Canadian people which spends increasing amounts of money, that is, $71 million this year.
Why must a body of that importance, which costs so much to the Canadian people, refuse to reply to simple questions asked by representatives of the people in this house?
Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask this- and the hon. members for St. Denis and Maisonneuve-Rosemont know very well I will have no reply this afternoon-why the minister should not have the power when we ask him a question, whether it be on the estimates or on the orders of the day, to reply on what goes on in that corporation? We asked questions, but got no answers.
We thought the Liberals were making a mistake in setting up that system. We thought they were indulging in a comfortable laziness by not dealing with that situation. But we, the newly elected representatives of the people, were sent to parliament in 1957 and in 1958 in order to bring about some changes. And we want to know the truth about the C.B.C., both in the interest of the C.B.C. itself and in the interest of the people.
The C.B.C. is the target of frequently unfounded criticisms. But how can we know, how can we know the truth, if not by demanding that C.B.C. officials reply to our questions? Otherwise they could be told: "If you do not want to reply, is it because you have something to hide?"
It is not by reading an enumeration of items on a page that we will understand what the C.B.C. proposes to do with the money it is asking us to vote. Nor is it by consulting its statement of assets and liabilities in the second book of public accounts, that we will find what use is being made of the peoples' money.
Supply-C.B.C.
A statement of assets and liabilities means nothing without details. More particularly when there is an unexplained deficit.
We are objecting to such proceedings, we want to know how the money paid to the C.B.C. has been used and what causes that deficit.
We ask the government to take a positive attitude in the matter, and to decide once for all whether crown corporations will remain independent of the people who must ultimately pay the piper and the deficits.
If those deficits are legitimate, if they can be explained-why does not the C.B.C. explain them? We should be satisfied. But why does the C.B.C. give no details in the public accounts as all other departments do with regard to their expenses?
Let there be the necessary reforms in the structure of the corporation-administrative reforms-but, at least, let there be a serious consideration of suggestions made by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay), as well as by the hon. member for Berthier (Mr. Paul) who quoted the public and departmental inquiries act, chapter 154 of the revised statutes of 1952.
Let us consider the proposal of the hon. member for Berthier.
I invite the hon. members for St. Denis and for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, to read over again the speeches of the representatives of Roberval and Berthier, before they criticize them. They will realize first of all to what extent they are unfair, and how stupid they can be in criticizing them.
Section 2	of chapter	154	of the	revisedstatutes of	1952	reads	as	follows:
The governor in council may, whenever he deems it expedient, cause inquiry to be made into and concerning any matter connected with the good government of Canada or the conduct of any part of the public business thereof.
I challenge the Liberals or the C.C.F. group to discover	any	defect	in	that legislation
which would enable the C.B.C. to elude such inquiry.
I contend that the government has the power, under this chapter, to launch an inquiry into the financial situation of the C.B.C.
If the hon. member for St. Denis wants to list the matters	to be discussed,	I shall

Supply-C.B.C.
tell him of a few. Subsequently, if he wishes to do so, he can ask the minister some questions.
For instance, let there be an inquiry about some people who are supposed to get double pay from the C.B.C.
Let there be an investigation into extravagance, like that expense of $1,000 not very long ago to bring a singer from Europe to Montreal who could have been asked to delay her departure.
Let there be an inquiry into those small cliques, into family compacts, and into all the pals, the boy friends, the girl friends, the mistresses. Let there be an inquiry into the cost of stage sets. What is the cost going to be of this or that T.V. dramatic presentation or of some other program referred to as a "continuity".
Let there be an inquiry into travelling expenses, not only for local performers-and I do not want to make any personal reference to Miss Germaine Dugas, who is one of our most talented French Canadian singers, and who deserves to be encouraged by the C.B.C., which corporation has, on the other hand no reason whatsoever to invite to its studios a burnt-out performer like Lucienne Boyer; but let there also be an inquiry on the travelling expenses of foreign performers.
The case of Miss Dugas should not be the only one examined, but also the travelling expenses of some foreign artists.
Last year in the committee on broadcasting, questions were asked to determine whether it was true that certain performers making a round of appearances in clubs, concert halls or theatres, that is to say, under private sponsorship, were getting double fees, or were being paid both by the impresarios and by the C.B.C., including travelling expenses.
We asked questions and got no answers.
For instance, we asked whether it was true that certain performers who had come to Canada under sponsorship of private interests, or impresarios, had had their travelling expenses paid, not only by their impresarios, but also by the C.B.C. Again, no answer was given to this question.
If the hon. member for St. Denis wants to enlighten himself he should look into the case of a particular club waiter, now a producer, who is a close friend of that patriarch Levesque, who is now a member of the Quebec legislature.

The way in which sponsors are forced to pick a particular program might also bear some looking into. We should be told whether our information is correct.
Mr. Chairman, we must find a way to start an investigation before the people rebel and decide that the C.B.C. is too costly and should be scrapped.
We must react before the people grow more indignant and demand that the government clean up the mess. We must straighten out what needs straightening. Let us have some answers now. Let it be a whitewashing if necessary, but let us have an investigation. Let us find out for sure if such situations exist.
Furthermore, let us be told about kickbacks. Again, we asked questions last year on this matter, but got no answer.
Some people who were producers before T.V. came in, are now supervisors or C.B.C. executives.
There have even been charges that such producers get kickbacks on the fees paid to C.B.C. actors or other performers.
Here again, no answer was given. We want to know the truth; we are seeking the light.
The C.B.C. is charged-could it be true?- with refusing sponsors, and keeping sponsorless programs on the air. We inquired about that, but again, no answer was given.
People talk of immorality within the C.B.C. I do not say that the expression is correct, I do not suggest that it is in keeping with the facts, but mention was made of this in Montreal and certainly in Toronto. Accusations of immorality have been made against the C.B.C. I am not shocked more than is necessary, but with the members of this house who are the least bit responsible, I say that this business must be cleared up because we have no right to let such accusations be made against the C.B.C. without doing anything about it. If it is true, then severe measures should be taken. If not, then the facts should be set in their true light, and this for the benefit of the C.B.C. We have the right as representatives of the people to restate those accusations and to say: Gentlemen of the C.B.C., shed light on the matter, hire a public relations officer who will try to defend you against those accusations, and account for your actions before parliament; but in the name of truth, in the

very interest of the C.B.C., we urge you to answer those questions.
Mention has been made of political recommendations. I do not know one Conservative member who can boast of having succeeded in placing someone with the C.B.C. I know that in my riding there are a great many people in the C.B.C.'s employment who earn their salary and are good servants of the corporation. I also know that some of them recruit other employees, while a member could not even recommend one person, though it be an unemployed person in dire poverty. A member of parliament cannot recommend anybody for employment with the C.B.C., because he would be accused of patronage and of filling the C.B.C. with Conservatives.
The member for Chambly-Rouville cannot recommend people to the C.B.C., but any moron, whether he be a sweeper or a clerk, can sometimes find a better job than his own for a friend, provided he has a minimum of qualifications. And this is done without examination, without any serious control, so that people are hired without examination or control.
We inquired about this in the committee on broadcasting, but we got no answer. We are inclined to believe, Mr. Chairman, that it is easier to find a job for a "chum", a "girl friend", or the mistress of this one or that one, for it seems that all too often physical attractiveness is the main consideration. At least that is what I have heard-I am only repeating what I have heard. I would like that to be brought to light. It is said that in some cases, physical attractiveness is often more important than intelligence or talent.
The report of the committee on radio and television broadcasting shows that we referred to the hiring of personnel last year and had questions to ask. As reported on page 784, I put the following question to Mr. Carter:
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, on a point of order, has this only been going on for half an hour?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The hon. member's time is not up yet.
(Translation):

Since it seems that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) would like to shorten my speech, I shall immediately mention something which concerns him. During the last electoral campaign, we heard people talk about contracts awarded without tenders, and it was said that there would be no more patronage in the awarding of those contracts.
Supply-C.B.C.
Last year, as reported at page 733 of the report of the committee on broadcasting, I put the following question to Mr. Richardson: (Text):
Coming back to the Radio Canada building, were public tenders called tor the construction of this building?

It has not been our practice to call for public tenders, if you mean by "public tenders", advertising in the press?
(Translation):
I would advise Mr. Lesage to take note of that answer. It will serve him as a basic formula, everywhere, to explain the patronage he is about to organize.
(Text):
Do I understand that there were tenders called?
We always call tenders for any construction.
Was the number limited of those who were asked to tender?

No, we usually start off-and this is actually covered by a different item-by having a list, and we endeavour to use local contractors wherever possible, that is, contractors in the community in which we propose to build. We invite a number, and this number varies; it may be six, three, or may be ten. Then, anyone else who wants to tender on it applies for the drawings, specifications, and so on. If he appears to be a reliable contractor who is capable of carrying out the work, we never have any objection to that.
I invite the attention of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate to the following passage:

Before 1957 did you have any protest from ministers of the crown or members of parliament against the way in which contracts were awarded, that is, without asking for public tenders by advertising in the papers?

I do not recall any such objections.
(Translation):
That was the practice of the C.B.C. Why should the Department of Public Works, the Department of Transport and every other department have to invite public tenders, and not the C.B.C.?
Could there be political patronage in such matters?
How are employees hired? The committee on broadcasting established that last year, when we discussed the system of subsidies and the matter of pull. Mention has been made of the movie "scandal". On many occasions last year, I asked questions on that subject. The committee lapsed, and I never got an answer, because every excuse under the sun was used to avoid answering my questions.
For instance, take the matter of paid advertisements in newspapers. I was told the

Supply-C.B.C.
C.B.C. places no paid ads in papers other than a particular newspaper on Notre Dame street, which has been campaigning for the Liberals. If that is not patronage, in the eyes of those Liberal gentlemen, I don't know what else it can be.
There was some talk about rentals of studios. Has any light been thrown on that matter? I would like this to be clarified.
And, finally, there are those cliques in the C.B.C. The corporation is charged with spreading Liberal and socialist propaganda. Has this charge been answered by the Liberals or by the C.B.C.? All they did was to charge us, the parliamentarians who want to know the truth, with creating hotbeds of Conservative intrigue. But, Mr. Chairman, I am not worried because we will have time to complete our 25 years of office before this happens.
But when a department submits its estimates and opposition members stand up for that department in connection with questions asked by members on the government benches, one has a feeling that there must be something queer and mysterious about it. There is certainly someone who wants to protect someone else, and it is not government people, it is not the responsible minister, nor the other ministers, nor government members; it is rather, as my colleague who is sitting here beside me said, those patronage people of the Liberal party, who do not want to lose their supporters. There is reference to cowardice in the C.B.C. We have-
(Text):

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must advise the hon. member that his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, I must say I followed the hon. member's speech closely through the translation system which is perhaps not fair to him but I believe he painted an exotic Parisian picture of the C.B.C. in Canada with his talk of the mistresses of certain people having more influence in getting jobs for people than members of parliament. We have had evidence in the committee with respect to the Jacques Cartier bridge which suggests that the influence of members of parliament when it was used seemed to indicate that they did not always have the best choice of prospects for jobs and the same might be true of the C.B.C. I think the hon. member has raised serious charges, the Parisian flavour of which I must say tantalized what I must describe as my worst self.
It is all over you.

Perhaps I should not proceed in that vein but it was most interesting. The

hon. gentleman brought up the points of Liberal and socialist propaganda and the fact that the C.B.C. in French Canada seemed to be that kind of agency. He seemed to indicate that because hon. members of the government from Quebec criticized the corporation and because hon. members of the Liberal party from Quebec praised or defended the C.B.C. there is something wrong, that there are patronage mongers. I cannot comment on that.
One of the targets of government members has been someone by the name of Rene Levesque. Several years ago he gave a series of programs on French Canadian culture over the English service of the C.B.C. These were well received. A number of my constituents have asked when we are going to see that likeable fellow again. I should like to suggest that if Mr. Levesque and another very charming French Canadian television personality, Maurice Lamontagne, cannot be used now on the French network because of their relationship perhaps the English service might plan some way of bringing them forward so we could benefit from their interpretation of culture.
We might get the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville.

Another point that interested me was this. I am pleased to see the number of government members who are making a contribution to this debate especially on the relationship of the C.B.C. in French Canada. I have often heard it argued that French Canadians should have more of their own in senior posts. If the fact that the head of the C.B.C. is one of their own has brought about this interest it is an encouraging thing and I believe something might be said for having more French Canadians in senior administrative posts.
I wish to express appreciation to a gentleman whom I note that the C.B.C. has promoted to Toronto, Mr. Michael Hind-Smith who was a producer here for a long time. My relations with him were never too friendly because we disagreed too strongly but I think he did a magnificent job especially on the royal visits and in terms of girding up or coaching politicians so they did not seem as bad as they really were when appearing on programs such as "the Nation's Business". I hope he will have success in his new position as manager of CBLT.
In the December 8, 1959 issue of the Clobe and Mail there was an interesting article entitled "Never Such Nonsense-Critics Contradictory, C.B.C. Chief Charges". The article reads in part:

The president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation said yesterday he has never heard or read so much uninformed nonsense about the C.B.C. as in the last month.
Mr. Ouimet is reported to have said:
Within the past month I have read or heard that the C.B.C. is wasteful; that private enterprise can provide the same service free; that broadcasting is primarily a vehicle for advertising; that Canada cannot afford Canadian programming; that there is no Canadian talent worth broadcasting, and that Canadians don't want Canadian programs.
X have never heard or read so much uninformed and negative nonsense in my life.
I think it is more than high time that somebody said something positive about Canadian broadcasting.
This sounds good to me and I hope it does to other hon. members. I hope that the minister and members of the board of broadcast governors and others in the C.B.C. will do some of this talking. I am glad the president kicked off on this line. 1 wish that those people who adumbrate general broadcasting policy would give us more of this. The article continues:
Mr. Ouimet said that "this destructive and negative mythology could, if unchecked, eventually threaten the effectiveness of our entire broadcasting system."
This was the point I made earlier, that there are these destructive forces and a trend which may lead to what has been applauded in this chamber, the break-up of the C.B.C. and its sale or partition to private interests. The article goes on:
The contradictory nature of the comment often floors us. On Monday we are too commercialized: on Tuesday, we should be more vigorously commercial; Wednesday the C.B.C. costs too much; Thursday the C.B.C. should extend its services; on Friday, too much culture; Saturday, too much sport; Sunday-well let's pretend it's a day of rest."
He said the corporation is not too worried because it is the kind of comment which usually balances itself out. But there is some "pretty fancy sophistry" going on, he said.
"About two weeks ago I sat in a public meeting at Ottawa and to my astonishment heard it said that the C.B.C. was established to do only those things which private stations couldn't do", Mr. Ouimet said. "And I think the speaker believed it."
This is what I wanted to come to.
That is what George Drew said.
I am pleased to hear that that was said by the former leader of the opposition and former leader of the government forces when they were in opposition. He also said some things about baby bonuses.
That is right.
The hon. member said that Canadian babies were better.

Those are Canadian babies. I
continue to quote:
Supply-C.B.C.
The C.B.C. was established, he said, to meet four basic principles of national broadcasting. To provide a complete broadcasting service; one which links all parts of Canada; one that is predominantly Canadian in content; one that serves French and English cultures equitably.
I should like to ask the minister whether he feels he and the government still subscribe to these four principles, and whether at the present time the principles are in any danger, or whether they are in need of change. I will just repeat the principles:
To provide a complete broadcasting service; one which links all parts of Canada; one that is predominantly Canadian in content; one that serves French and English cultures equitably.
"These are really the basic considerations. And yet you see very little of them in print these days and they are too infrequently heard in any discussion of Canadian broadcasting."
I have been trying to serve the intent of Mr. Ouimet on this occasion by giving this another airing when we are in the middle of the discussion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation estimates. I should like to reiterate what I asked before. Can we have from the minister his assessment of these basic principles in relation to the trends and what seemed to be a portent in his speech last year at this time that there was going to have to be a reconsideration of this private set-up further along the way? It seems to me that it is far enough along the way. The board of broadcast governors announced the ground rules for the network-
They have not announced the ground rules; they have only been proposed for discussion in a meeting, as the hon. member knows.
I saw one newspaper heading which said that the B.B.G. had announced the ground rules; they are tentative ground rules.
It shows how unreliable headings are sometimes.

Some of us wonder whether it is the headings, the news services of the B.B.G. that is unreliable, but we are dealing with the C.B.C. now.
One of the points that bothers me is the petty one that has to do with the complaint I saw in a Toronto paper recently by Film Editorial Services Limited. I have here a copy of the letter they sent to Dr. Stewart of the board of broadcast governors. In general they have a complaint about a film they produced and the failure of the C.B.C. to buy it. I just wish to say that according to their argument the C.B.C. looks pretty small in so far as this particular set of films is concerned. The C.B.C. seem rather hurt that they were not informed of our intention to shoot this series, and even more hurt to find that not only do we complete it, but that it is better than their own products.
The C.B.C. is wrong in assuming that the B.B.C. is taking only the visuals, they are in fact supplied with international tracks and scripts as is normal in an overseas transaction.
During our talks with the C.B.C. nothing was said to indicate that our films were unacceptable as network material, on the contrary, we got as far as talking about two network plays, over a period of two years, and later about placing them in a program such as "Junior Magazine," which is of course a network show in itself.
If the CJB.C. had no intention of entering into a deal with us, why did they waste our time and efforts for almost a year before giving us an answer neither positive nor negative. If the problem is as they say, one of money, then surely they knew this six months ago, and even then all we asked for was an agreement to rent, not instant money.
I am always aware that there are two sides to every story and every argument, but this particular side is very well put and it does make the C.B.C. look as sensitive, as prickly and as indecisive as it has been labelled at times today by certain speakers.
I should like to have from the minister some explanation regarding this particular matter. I should also like to know from him what has been done about programming in the Windsor area? We have a real problem there, or so I am informed. I want to bring this up in detail later on the B.B.G. estimates.
Of course the residents of the Windsor area have many television and radio channels available to them. The big local station in Windsor, CKLW, is largely United States-owned; the newscasts are United States oriented and much of their programming has that orientation, so much so that I gather the station was brought before the board of broadcast governors last fall and asked for an explanation.
The C.B.C. has a service in the Windsor area, but the complaint about it is that it is not local enough and not geared enough to the local community to get the kind of audience and to have the kind of reception that one would expect. As a consequence, some people in the Windsor area have complained to me that they are in perhaps the most vulnerable position in Canada to United States influence. If the C.B.C. is a cultural body and wants to perform a service it can do so by taking a keener part in the Windsor area. I should like to know whether this has ever been a consideration of the C.B.C.?
One last point I wish to return to is the financing of the C.B.C. I understand the

hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate brought it up and it had been brought up repeatedly. The minister's argument last year was that this government has been more generous to the C.B.C. The argument for the situation where the C.B.C. does not have to come every year before treasury board and fight for its funds is that it is given more freedom. This particular principle is always extolled in Britain in connection with the
B.	B.C. and with the university grants board; the idea being of getting some kind of projection and knowing that within a fairly extended period of time, such as half a decade, what your capital requirements are going to be and how much you are going to spend so you can plan.

I know that at the time the C.B.C. was before the treasury board last fall I inquired from the minister and at the time the C.B.C. was in front of the treasury board I telephoned the C.B.C. officials to find out about extension of services and they said they could not really tell until they were through with treasury board. I phoned afterwards and I know some hon. members have been in touch with them about possible extension of services and we got no better answer. The only thing we were told was that the
C.	B.C. was left with some latitude within its budget by treasury board as to how it would expend its money. Mr. Chairman, I did not know, when the discussion was interrupted at five o'clock that I would have the pleasure of taking up this matter again so soon.

Supply-C.B.C.
This morning, I listened to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). According to him, the representatives of the people want to have some detailed information with regard to questions which have been asked. I entirely agree with the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm. A member of this house has a right to ask questions and to receive clear and precise answers that will enable him to get an idea of the expenses or improvements that should be made in any branch or division.
He was asked why he did not take the opportunity to ask his questions. He resorted to all sorts of evasions to say that it was not the proper time to do so.
Yet we know that if we have questions to ask about the C.B.C. there is no better time than this.
Even if the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. McCleave), is substituting for the minister responsible for the C.B.C., we know that all the needed staff is available to answer our questions adequately.
Personally, I think the member for Halifax has all the qualifications for a cabinet post.
Mr. Chairman, the ineffable member for Roberval (Mr. Tremblay) raised a number of questions. He said the C.B.C. has refused to provide details. I am wondering whether that is true. I think the corporation is prepared to supply details. Some have already been made available. There may have been cases where the corporation appeared somewhat reluctant.
I think that hon. members, whether they be government or opposition members, have the right to press for required information.
Mr. Chairman, the member for Roberval said that the C.B.C. is much more vulnerable than other departments because this corporation is concerned with the minds and the conscience of men. He recalled the moral principles of philosophy and theology that were involved in those productions. It is certainly not a bad thing that a member take issue with the C.B.C. on this matter. I repeat that it is his right to do so.
However, where I differ in opinion with the ineffable member for Roberval is when he poses as the sole and only censor of everything that goes on in that corporation. In fact, I wonder if, in spite of his polished language, he has the required qualifications to act as the official censor for the province of Quebec.

Besides, the C.B.C. is not only intended for the province of Quebec. Its very name is a clear indication of this: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It is for the whole country.
We might find fault with the C.B.C.
I think that if we could put a question to Mr. Ouimet to which he could supply an answer, he would do so willingly. He would admit himself, besides, that nothing in this world is perfect, no more in the C.B.C., where programs are so complicated and complex than anywhere else.
But to go so far as to say, as did some members, that everything is to be condemned, that is going a little too far.
I know that the member for Roberval is keenly interested in the C.B.C. and that he claims the corporation has infringed upon certain rights in the field of education.
Again I feel that this is going too far.
The C.B.C. had certainly the right in its own field to organize certain courses which proved to be very interesting, very instructive and from which we learned a lot.
If the hon. members who criticized those courses had followed them, they undoubtedly would have increased their scientific and even philosophic knowledge. In fact, we had first class programs.
Does that constitute interference in the field of education? I do not think so. Those were not compulsory courses. Nobody was obliged to listen.
Thanks to those programs, people who had finished school could add to their knowledge.
In my opinion, no provision in the constitution forbids the C.B.C. from broadcasting such programs of great help to those who have left school or university.
Besides, I know that when those C.B.C. programs started they were under the direction of Mr. Aurele Seguin who is now Rev. Father Aurele Seguin, dominican.
I am convinced that, on account of his knowledge and in addition to his religious convictions, Mr. Seguin was qualified to prepare those programs which will never come in conflict with the conscience of our hon. members.
Those responsible for these programs have been congratulated by people in Canada and abroad.
Therefore, I feel that the C.B.C. is entirely justified in presenting such programs which

increase the knowledge of our fellow citizens and that it cannot be accused of infringing upon the field of education.
There are also programs of a scientific nature, which are prepared by another Mr. Seguin whose first name I cannot recall. Those programs are a mine of information and enable you to grasp things that remained hazy, even after school or university. Those programs gave me the impression that even the most difficult things could be made easy. Instead of criticizing the C.B.C., we should congratulate it.
As the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said, when artists or television people, such as Rene Levesque are not wanted in the province of Quebec, they are picked up and give a good account of themselves in other parts of the country.
Mr. Levesque is a worker. He puts in long hours of research to prepare a program, and gets accurate data to support his statements.
As far as Mr. Seguin is concerned, he was asked to repeat in English the programs he had produced on the French network, and apparently, the English element is quite happy about it.
So, it would be in absolute bad taste to say such programs are contrary to the Canadian constitution because they deal with science. That does not mean they encroach upon the field of education, which is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
I repeat that the C.B.C. has been doing a very good job in this field. On the other hand, if there are weak spots, let us hear about them. If some have requests to make, let them speak up. If they want figures, let the figures be supplied. Any member, whether in the opposition or on the government side, is entitled to such information.
However, I cannot condone unwarranted criticism. Criticism should be based on serious information.
The hon. member for Roberval has asked for a royal commission.
In view of the many questions raised by some government members, namely the hon. members for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Johnson), St. Mary (Mr. Valade), Roberval and even Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul), I think so many doubts have been raised that it might be good to have a royal commission rather than to let a committee of the house inquire into C.B.C. operations.
There is now a committee of the house which includes representatives of the three political parties, which of course have political interests to protect.
Besides, a royal commission of inquiry does not deal with political criticism.

I intend to name a few of them, and if I forget a few names, I would ask the minister to give me the same information about them. I refer in particular to Messrs. Wilfrid Lemoyne, Gerard Pelletier, Rene Levesque and Mrs. Judith Jasmin.
Second, I would ask the minister whether Mr. Dostaler O'Leary is still the permanent representative of the C.B.C. French network in Paris.
Third, if Mr. O'Leary is still the permanent representative in Europe, why is he not in a position to make any reports, rather than compelling the C.B.C. to send to Europe Messrs. Wilfrid Lemoyne, Gerard Pelletier

and Rene Levesque, as well as Mrs. Judith Jasmin who, after such a long trip, must rest and then go back again.
Wilfrid Lemoyne, Rene Levesque, Gerard Pelletier; the following month, Mrs. Judith Jasmin, Rene Levesque, Gerard Pelletier, Phillippe Lemoyne, always the same group, always the same favourites, always the same gang, as they say in politics.
As to the broadcast on refugees in the "Premier plan" series, I should like to ask a question to C.B.C. officials. Who is in charge of cultural programs and of the so-called public affairs panel discussions? I should like to know who, in the "Premier plan" series, was responsible for last Sunday's broadcast, when Mrs. Judith Jasmin interviewed people and discussed immigration in connection with the refugee year? Who is responsible for that broadcast, and who authorized Mrs. Jasmin to take that opportunity to recall some sharp criticism directed at present government policy on immigration. I do not deny Mrs. Jasmin's right to express any opinion, just as I recognize that any commentator has a right to his opinion. What I do object to, is that the C.B.C. should have a right to foist upon the people of Quebec and Canada, at least on the French network, always the same commentators and people of the same school; people from Cite libre, La Reforme, Le Devoir, or other publications of the same school. Why always the same commentators? I refuse to believe there are no commentators with different ideas or opinions.
I do not want to mention names, but I see now in the press gallery a commentator who should be invited more often on the C.B.C. I wonder if his unbiased attitude stands in the way of his obtaining engagements.
Here is another case, again in the same context; we ask who is responsible in the C.B.C. for selecting commentators. We object to the C.B.C. imposing commentators or moderators for quiz programs and panels, to the C.B.C. imposing supporters of the Conservatives, the Union Nationale, the Social Credit, the Liberal or the C.C.F. parties. We simply ask that moderators be known for their impartiality. I do not know that Mr. Jean-Louis Gagnon, who has been the Liberal party publicist until recently is an impartial moderator as regards provincial or federal politics.
In passing, I would like to mention another example. There was much talk about a re-79951-0-379J

broadcast of an emergency session of the United Nations after the break-down of the summit conference. When the situation was extremely serious and when, more than ever before, the western nations had to unite and work together, there was a special program of commentaries in which Mr. Naim Kathan, Mr. Jean-Louis Gagnon and Mr. Andre Lau-rendeau took part. They took advantage of this opportunity for a bitter attack on the policy of the United States and that of their allies, including Canada itself. I think that they fell with a sort of sadistic relish on the speech delivered at the United Nations by the delegate of the United States, Mr. Henry Cabot Lodge and they mentioned its shortcomings. But they had words of praise for Mr. Gromyko. Let us say once again that these people have a right to their own opinion. They were entitled to express it. No one is going to deny them this right. I find Mr. Andre Laurendeau a very interesting commentator, but I deplore the fact that, for an obvious reason, Mr. Rene Levesque, should have to part with C.B.C., because I imagine that the C.B.C. will be honest enough to let go of the new minister of public works and hydraulic resources as I would hope that the new minister will want to devote all his time to his department.
I found Mr. Levesque interesting and I do not deny that he has the right to come to the C.B.C. to express his views, as have Mr. Jean-Louis Gagnon, Mr. Andre Laurendeau, and all those other writers who are counting on C.B.C. fees to supplement their miserable salaries. I have no quarrel with all these people, because they have a right to their opinions. Moreover, if they are invited to appear on television, I admit that they are entitled to say what they think.
What is wrong is not that those men should express their views, but the fact that the freedom of the city is thus given to individuals who all belong to the same clique, to people who protect and help one another in obtaining positions, and who do everything they can to exclude others from those jobs or from the possibility of appearing on the telescreens; who are doing their utmost to stop those who do not belong to their school of thought from being seen and heard on our networks.
We should like to be told by the director of programs, or the official in charge-that is the director of cultural programs-or the producer of these programs, or any people responsible for those public affairs interviews, why only representatives of a single school of thought are invited to appear.

Supply-C.B.C.
As I say, it is not the people who freely express their views that are responsible, but those who take it upon themselves always to invite people of the same school. This happens over and over again, for they always approach these persons of the same trend of thought, without ever finding out whether it would not be possible to ask people who do not share those views. Consequently, whenever a program on any subject is given, generally two or three people of the same school of thought are asked, for instance, Messrs. Levesque, Laurendeau and Gagnon, whereas there is only one person defending the opposite view. We do not have to give the dates or facts about such and such a day when that happened, for one has only to look at television sometimes to know what happens on the French network.
Unfortunately, I have not got the time to ask other questions, but I say it is time the C.B.C. took a good look at that field of public affairs programs. The C.B.C. has a responsibility, not only a legal one, towards parliament and the Canadian government, but also a moral responsibility towards the Canadian people and the French network, and in particular towards the French speaking population.
The C.B.C. has no right to sidestep issues. It must see to it that all opinions voiced on its network are voiced freely. An inquiry into the C.B.C. must be undertaken at all costs. If those statements that I have just repeated are inaccurate, let us have some evidence that we are wrong, let us have facts at the inquiry to prove the contrary. But let us have something, some explanation, and not that silence of complicity.
I would like to make only one comment about what the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) said after the first part of my remarks. I was under the impression, on hearing the hon. member for Port Arthur, that he was enjoying one of his numerous intellectual thrills he gets when the French Canadians, here in this house, are snapping at each other and telling each other a few home truths. I should like to point out to the hon. member for Port Arthur that the French network has perhaps its faults. He may laugh at it. He may laugh at the fact that we have the courage of airing them in the open, or at least of asking questions in the house. But he should not rejoice too quickly. I suggest that the English network is not without fault either. However, I have the decency to leave it to those who are more competent than I am to talk about it.
If the hon. member for Port Arthur wants to make fun of the French network inferring by this that everything is well in the English network, that is his own business. As for

me, I must make an important remark. There is nothing odious in unfolding the faults of the French network. I have been a member of this house for two years and this is our third session. I refrained for three years from making the remarks I made today. The facts I reported are only rumours and accusations that are repeated everywhere. They are nothing new because they were being made even before I was a member of this house. They were even stronger under the Liberal administration. But I wilfully refrained from dealing with this matter here because I hoped that the C.B.C. would manage to mend its ways, because I was hoping that, following the establishment of a committee on broadcasting such as the one which sat last year, and the report submitted afterwards, the C.B.C. would go out of its way to rectify certain situations. Well, I find that there are deficiencies to be corrected yet and I believe, or at least I feel, that we are entitled to come in this house and ask whether it would not be possible to launch an inquiry in order to ascertain whether such accusations are founded or not.
Not only is the reputation of the C.B.C. at stake, but the reputation of the French network, something with which I am particularly concerned.
Again, I am not blaming anyone, because if I quoted names, or laid specific charges, I might needlessly smear some people. In a committee, the Liberals could easily indulge in witch hunting, so I would rather have a royal commission to inquire into the financial situation of the C.B.C., where anyone charged would have a chance to defend himself. Those who claim I am wrong in taking this stand should recall what happened last year in the committee on broadcasting. First of all, every hon. member knows, or rather has observed that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate started making obstructions from the outset, giving the impression that he feared too close scrutiny of what went on in the C.B.C. under the Liberal government. It was not so.
Immediately the words "witch hunt" were bandied about, and from the very minute a certain C.B.C. official in Toronto threatened to go on strike or resign, on the grounds that there had been political interference in the administration of the C.B.C., Liberal members jumped at the chance and tried to smear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) and even the Prime Minister, charging them with political interference,

something which has never been proven. Who, Mr. Chairman, were the witch hunters in the broadcasting committee during the 1959 session, the Conservatives or the Liberals? At the very outset, we indicated that we wanted to ask questions, and that is my reply to the member for Hull (Mr. Caron). In the committee, you could not insinuate without laying a charge. You could not ask questions, because by some sleight of hand, a rule had been passed preventing us from asking certain questions. Indeed, under a rule which had been passed in my absence, discussion was restricted in such a way that whenever we attempted to ask questions, we were told that the people involved could not answer, that we could not delve into personalities, that we could not ask certain questions. The chairman of the committee was bound by that rule.
We had no chance of proving anything at that time. We wanted to hear and question a number of personalities, including Rene Levesque, one of the leaders of the C.B.C. strike in 1959. All kinds of people were being summoned to Ottawa, it was like a kind of pilgrimage, but we were not allowed to question them, so the committee was ineffective. It was like attending an investigation on a car accident. The accused came to testify and was asked questions on the accident, but while admitting his ownership of the car, he would reply that he knew nothing of the accident because someone else had been driving. All they could reply were statements of principle seeking to indicate that all was well in the C.B.C., that everything was functioning perfectly, that there was nothing wrong, and that everything was all right in the C.B.C., that no criticisms was deserved. But we were allowed to ask questions dealing, for instance, with the cost of such and such a program.
Mr. Chairman, once again, we never tried to do some witch hunting in the committee on broadcasting or in this house last year. We had to mention charges that had been laid outside parliament against the C.B.C. When we did that, the Liberals told us to ask specific questions, and when, in committee, we wanted to ask specific questions to certain officials, we were told that those gentlemen could not answer because we would be making personal references, and tarnishing reputations. If the C.B.C. is to be scrutinized, this should be done through an inquiry. This is the only way to dispel any unfounded ac-

cusation. And those who lay those accusations against the C.B.C., either in newspapers or elsewhere, should be given the opportunity to prove them or should remain silent.

I just wish to ask the
minister whether, after this trilogy, he does not think there was a lot of force in my view that the C.B.C. should have a five-year budget?

Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. has had a thorough going over in this recent debate. I should like to go on record as a person who believes the C.B.C. has done a good job. This is not an unqualified endorsement of all its actions. I do believe that in so far as an organization dealing with ideas and entertainment is concerned, the sum and substance of this type of operation must be such that there is a variance in views. I remember an article by that eminent member of the press gallery, Mr. Blakely. It was on the C.B.C. He has written many on the C.B.C. Incidentally this one had to do with political partisanship of the C.B.C. He said the C.B.C. was roundly condemned by the Conservatives, the Liberals and the C.C.F., in turn, as being the spokesman of opposing parties.
I do believe the C.B.C. is in a transitional stage. At one time they were judge, jury and prosecutor; they made their own rules and regulations; they ran broadcasting in Canada with an unquestioned and iron hand. That has been changed and the changes which have been made are for the good. I think those changes have received support from all sides of the house.
The C.B.C. is now doing the job which the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned namely that of maintaining a Canadian identity, promoting a Canadian culture and knitting together this country. Even if it is not quite as broad in miles as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate said, it is still pretty large.
May I pose a question to the hon. member? Has he ever measured the distance from the farthest west point of the Yukon to Cape Bonavista?

That is a diagonal split.

Supply-C.B.C.
I hope I am pouring a little bit of oil on troubled waters. Many hon. members, including my friends from Kootenay East and Kootenay West and also other hon. members who have problems which I have not, want greater coverage of television and radio, radio first and then television, for the remote areas of this country. This is a job that only the C.B.C. can do. If we were to apply the same philosophy to air lines then Canadian Pacific Air Lines would be operating all the well travelled routes and the feeder lines would be relegated to T.C.A. The argument seems to have been that any money spent on outlets in big cities is wasted because it has not been spent in bringing the benefits of the C.B.C. to remote areas. I think there must be a balance between the remote areas and city coverage. It is just as important to promote Canadianism in the cities, and considering that most of our new Canadians flock to the cities it is perhaps a little more important than it is to bring entertainment and the Canadian viewpoint to remote areas.
Within the balance of the funds available and having regard to the job to be done I think that the C.B.C. is doing a relatively fair job at present. I believe there is a lot of merit in the idea that they could be more open about their affairs. Possibly they do not know themselves but I think they should at least have an idea as to how much their capital budgets will be in succeeding years and I think they could develop a program so that people would know that if service was not coming this year they were at least on the list for the next year. If they do this, of course, they will subject themselves to pressure from those areas that are four or five years away on the list, and perhaps it is with that viewpoint in mind that they are keeping away from setting out any long range plan although they may have one.
I wish to point out that if we are going to kick about the budget of the C.B.C. then we cannot at the same time ask for extra stations because extra stations represent not only capital costs but operating costs and the operating costs are continuing costs. Therefore if we want to have more service we must provide more money.
I am all in favour of the competition the C.B.C. is getting in the major centres across the country and in many cities which would not be called major centres but where there is a logical outlet for a private station. I think this is all to the good. I am indeed pleased that in Vancouver we are to have a new station. I was very disappointed at the amount of money that went across the line for advertising. I would sooner watch an

independent Canadian station than a United States station particularly as we can control the program content.
However, with all the good will in the world I think the C.B.C. almost has a genius for putting its foot in its mouth in that at periodic intervals it seems to arouse storms of controversy. I do not want to go back into history but I might refer to the appearance of the corporation before a committee of the house last year. Certain members on the other side of the house did not seem to think the committee did a good job but I think it was one of the better committees of the house although I was not a member of it. In spite of that, I think they did a good job.
The amount of money contributed by sponsors, for instance, in relation to the total cost of programs was a shock to me and to the people of Canada generally. The lack of liaison between the upper brass and the operating people in the various centres was another unsatisfactory situation. I do not know whether it has been corrected but it certainly was a drawback to the efficient operation of a corporation of the size of the C.B.C., with the diverse problems that face the corporation. Perhaps in the re-organization there has been a strengthening of these weak spots and an opening of lines of communication with the result that the corporation may be operating in a more efficient and effective manner than it was before.
But in spite of all the things that can be said about the C.B.C. it is my opinion that in general the C.B.C. has done a good job. I have received letters complaining about C.B.C. programs. If the C.B.C. acted on every letter I have received about programs there would not be any C.B.C. programs because everybody is going to complain about some program. That is the way the situation happens to be. We are not regimented to the point where we all think the same and all have the same tastes.
I am afraid I am not contributing too much to this debate but I do wish to ask for some degree of fair play and reasonableness in our consideration of the job that has to be done. Let us consider the job that has been done in relation to what there is to do. Mistakes have been made, and I am sure the officials of the C.B.C. will be the first to admit that.
There is one thing that strikes me as being another instance of the corporation putting its foot in its mouth, but perhaps this may be the last time this complaint will be made. I refer to the fact that we have heard criticism today that all we have before us is one item of $62 million. I suppose the C.B.C. has a financial statement and report in the same way as the C.N.R. which would

give details of the $62 million and how it is to be spent. The details are not in the book of estimates but will be in the report of the corporation. Why in heaven's name does the corporation not have enough forethought to have these documents ready for the time when the minister has to bring the estimates of the corporation before the House of Commons? If I am being unjust in this comment I will beg the corporation's pardon, but if what I have said is true I think they have also put the minister in a rather bad spot. Of course, as I say again, it is not done deliberately and has just happened this way but it is in line with the proclivity of the corporation to make rather silly mistakes. In spite of that, Mr. Chairman, I say again that I think the C.B.C. warrants the support of the house and the people of the country generally.

Mr. Chairman, after a day of verbal blasts at the C.B.C. by many of us I think a compliment is possibly in order. The few brief remarks I wish to make are related to some of the comments that have been made by various members today with regard to programs. It has been said today that in programming the C.B.C. should put more emphasis on Canadianism. I think the minister and the officials of the C.B.C. will be very pleased to know that during the past week the corporation saw fit to send a very capable team of cameramen, program directors and commentators to Flin Flon to shoot a few thousand feet of film of the events associated with the fabulous Flin Flon trout festival. These men did a remarkable job, and I really believe that the results of their efforts will provide great enjoyment and be of educational value to people in all parts of Canada. I can assure the minister that their efforts were greatly appreciated by the people of Flin Flon and the hardworking directors of the Flin Flon trout festival.
